recipes.name: Cacio e pepe
recipes.description: Rome's three-ingredient pasta: spaghetti or tonnarelli tossed with finely grated Pecorino Romano, toasted black pepper and starchy pasta water until it turns into a smooth, clinging cream.

ingredients.name: Pecorino Romano
ingredients.prep: very finely grated, at room temperature

steps.t: Grate the pecorino as finely as you can (a microplane gives a powdery snow) into a mixing bowl and leave it to come to room temperature; cold, coarse cheese clumps instead of melting. Crush the peppercorns coarsely in a mortar or under a heavy pan.

Bring about 3 litres of water to the boil in the large pot and salt it lightly, less than usual, because pecorino is already salty. Using less water than normal makes the cooking water starchier, and that starch is what turns the cheese into a sauce.
Add the pasta and stir for the first minute so the strands don't stick. Set a timer for 2 minutes less than the packet time.

Meanwhile toast the pepper in the dry frying pan over medium heat, shaking the pan, until it smells warm and fragrant, about 1 minute. Add a ladle (about 150 ml) of the pasta water and let it simmer gently.

Make the cheese cream: add about 100 ml of hot but not boiling pasta water to the pecorino a little at a time, mashing with a fork or small whisk into a thick, smooth paste like yoghurt. If it turns stringy the water was too hot; let the next splashes cool for a moment.

Lift the pasta with tongs straight into the pepper pan, bringing some water with it. Toss over medium heat for 1–2 minutes, adding splashes of cooking water, until the pasta is just al dente and coated in a starchy, peppery liquid.

Take the pan off the heat and wait about 30 seconds, until it has stopped sizzling. Add the cheese paste and toss vigorously with the tongs, adding pasta water a spoonful at a time, until the sauce is glossy and creamy and clings to every strand. Working off the heat matters: pecorino seizes into lumps when it gets too hot.
Serve immediately in warm bowls with a little extra pecorino and a final grind of pepper. The sauce tightens within minutes, so don't let it wait.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away; the sauce turns claggy as it cools. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently in a pan with a splash of water, tossing until hot; it won't be as creamy as when fresh.
notes: Pecorino Romano is a salty sheep's-milk cheese made with animal rennet. Parmigiano Reggiano gives a milder, sweeter sauce and works the same way.
If the sauce clumps, add a splash of warm water and keep tossing off the heat.

recipes.name: Spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino
recipes.description: The classic late-night Neapolitan pasta: spaghetti tossed with olive oil slowly infused with sliced garlic and dried chilli, emulsified with a little pasta water and finished with parsley.

steps.t: Bring about 4 litres of water to the boil in the large pot and salt it generously; it should taste pleasantly salty. Add the spaghetti, stir for the first minute so the strands don't stick, and cook for 1 minute less than the packet time.

While the pasta cooks, put the oil and sliced garlic into the cold frying pan and set it over medium-low heat. Starting cold lets the garlic flavour the oil slowly. Cook for 3–4 minutes, swirling the pan, until the garlic is pale golden at the edges and smells sweet. Don't let it brown: burnt garlic is bitter and you would have to start again.

Add the chilli and swirl for 20 seconds, then pour in a ladle (about 100 ml) of the pasta water to stop the garlic cooking; it will spit, so stand back. Keep the pan at a gentle simmer until the pasta is ready.

Lift the spaghetti with tongs straight into the frying pan, with the water that clings to it. Toss over medium-high heat for 1–2 minutes, adding more pasta water a splash at a time, until the oil and water come together into a light, cloudy sauce that coats the strands instead of pooling in the pan.
Take the pan off the heat, toss through the parsley, then taste and add salt if needed. A thin thread of raw olive oil over the top adds fragrance.
Serve at once in warm bowls. Neapolitans don't add cheese; a spoonful of toasted breadcrumbs is the traditional crunchy topping if you want one.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a frying pan with a splash of water, tossing until hot.
notes: Use the best olive oil you have; it is the sauce.

recipes.name: Pasta alla Norma
recipes.description: Catania's celebrated pasta: fried aubergine and a garlicky tomato and basil sauce tossed with short pasta and finished with plenty of salty grated ricotta salata.

ingredients.name: Ricotta salata
ingredients.prep: coarsely grated (or a firm, dry feta)

steps.t: Toss the aubergine cubes with the teaspoon of salt in a colander and leave over the sink for 20–30 minutes; this draws out water so they fry crisp and absorb less oil. Pat them thoroughly dry with kitchen paper. Small, firm aubergines can go straight into the pan.

Heat the oil in the large frying pan over medium-high heat until a cube of aubergine sizzles at once (about 180 °C). Fry the aubergine in two batches, turning often, until deep golden on all sides and creamy inside, 6–8 minutes per batch. Crowding the pan makes them steam and turn greasy. Drain on kitchen paper.
Pour off all but about 2 tablespoons of the oil. Lower the heat to medium-low, add the garlic and cook for 1–2 minutes, stirring, until fragrant and only just golden.
Add the passata, a good pinch of salt and half the basil. Simmer uncovered for 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce has thickened and a little oil glistens on the surface.
Meanwhile cook the pasta in plenty of well-salted boiling water until al dente. Scoop out a mug of the cooking water before draining.
Stir about two-thirds of the fried aubergine into the sauce. Add the drained pasta and toss over low heat for 1 minute, loosening with a splash of pasta water so the sauce coats every piece.
Serve in warm bowls topped with the remaining aubergine, a generous snowfall of grated ricotta salata and the rest of the basil.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Ricotta salata is a firm, salted, aged ricotta; a dry feta or Pecorino is the usual substitute outside Italy.
For a lighter version, toss the aubergine cubes with 3 tablespoons of oil and roast them at 220 °C for 25 minutes instead of frying.

recipes.name: Trofie al pesto genovese (with potatoes and green beans)
recipes.description: Genoa's way with pesto: short twisted trofie cooked in the same pot as potatoes and green beans, then tossed with a fresh pesto of basil, pine nuts, garlic, cheese and olive oil.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or small food processor

ingredients.name: Fresh basil leaves (small-leaved Genovese if possible)
Waxy potato (1 medium)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 1 cm slices

ingredients.name: Green beans
ingredients.prep: trimmed and cut into 4 cm lengths

steps.t: Bring a large pot of water to the boil and salt it well. You will cook the potatoes, pasta and beans in it one after another.

Make the pesto in the mortar: pound the garlic with the coarse salt to a paste, then add the pine nuts and pound until creamy. Add the basil a handful at a time and grind it with a circular motion against the sides of the mortar, rather than bashing, until the leaves break down into a bright green paste, 5–8 minutes. The salt crystals help tear the leaves.

Stir in both cheeses, then trickle in the oil, stirring with the pestle, until you have a loose, glossy sauce. In a processor, pulse the garlic, pine nuts and salt, then add the basil and oil and pulse in short bursts; running the blade continuously heats the basil and turns it dark and bitter. Stir in the cheese by hand.

Drop the potato slices into the boiling water. After 4 minutes add the dried trofie and stir. After another 5 minutes add the green beans and cook for 5–6 minutes more, until the pasta is al dente, the potatoes are tender and the beans are bright green and just soft.

Before draining, scoop out a mug of the cooking water. Put the pesto in the warm serving bowl and loosen it with 2–3 tablespoons of the hot water. Never heat pesto in a pan: it loses its colour and fragrance.
Drain the pasta and vegetables, tip them into the bowl and toss well. Some of the potato will break up and make the sauce creamy; add another splash of water if it looks dry.
Serve at once, with extra grated cheese at the table.

recipes.storage: Leftover pesto keeps for 3 days in the fridge under a thin layer of oil, or 3 months frozen (stir in the cheese after thawing). Refrigerate dressed pasta within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Eat leftovers at room temperature, or warm very gently with a splash of water without letting the pesto boil.
notes: Parmigiano and Pecorino are made with animal rennet; use vegetarian hard cheeses if needed.
In a hurry, use about 160 g of good fresh pesto from the chiller cabinet.

recipes.name: Pizza margherita
recipes.description: Naples' tricolour pizza: a soft, blistered dough topped with raw crushed tomatoes, fresh mozzarella, basil and olive oil, baked as hot as your oven will go.
equipment: Baking steel, pizza stone or heavy upturned baking tray
Pizza peel or a flat, rimless tray

ingredients.name: Tipo 00 or strong white bread flour
Whole peeled plum tomatoes (San Marzano type)
ingredients.prep: drained of excess juice and crushed by hand

steps.t: Make the dough: stir the yeast into the water in the large bowl, add about half the flour and mix, then add the salt and the rest of the flour and mix to a shaggy dough. Turn it onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic: it should spring back slowly when poked and stretch thin enough to see light through without tearing.

Put the dough back in the bowl, cover and leave at room temperature for about 2 hours, until doubled. For more flavour and an easier stretch, leave it 1 hour at room temperature and then up to 48 hours in the fridge.
Divide the dough into 4 pieces of about 205 g. Shape each into a taut ball by tucking the edges underneath, set them on a floured tray, cover and leave for about 1 hour, until puffy and relaxed.

Put the steel or stone on the top shelf of the oven, about 10–15 cm below the grill, and heat the oven to its maximum (250–280 °C) for at least 45 minutes. A thoroughly heated stone is what blisters the base.
Season the crushed tomatoes with the salt and 1 tablespoon of the oil; Neapolitan pizza sauce is not cooked beforehand. Pat the mozzarella dry with kitchen paper, because wet cheese floods the pizza.

Stretch one ball on a floured surface: press from the centre outwards with your fingertips, leaving a 1.5 cm rim untouched, then lift it and stretch it gently over your knuckles to 25–28 cm. Don't use a rolling pin; it presses out the air that makes the rim puff.

Lay the base on the floured peel. Spread 3–4 tablespoons of tomato thinly, leaving the rim bare, scatter over a quarter of the mozzarella and a couple of basil leaves and drizzle with a little oil. Work quickly so the dough doesn't stick to the peel.

Slide the pizza onto the stone and bake for 6–9 minutes, switching on the grill for the last 1–2 minutes if the top needs colour, until the rim is puffed and charred in spots and the cheese is melted and bubbling.
Finish with fresh basil and a thread of oil, slice and eat straight away. Let the stone reheat for 5 minutes before baking each of the remaining pizzas.

recipes.storage: Best eaten hot. Refrigerate leftover slices within 2 hours and eat within 2 days. Raw dough balls keep 2 days in the fridge or 1 month in the freezer.
recipes.reheating: Reheat slices in a covered dry frying pan over medium heat for 4–5 minutes, until the base is crisp and the cheese has melted.
notes: Mozzarella is usually made with animal rennet; check the label if that matters to you.

recipes.name: Focaccia genovese
recipes.description: Liguria's flat olive-oil bread: soft and open inside, golden and crisp underneath, with deep dimples that hold a salty brine of oil and water.

ingredients.name: Strong white bread flour or Tipo 0
Extra virgin olive oil
ingredients.prep: half for the dough, half for the tray

steps.t: Stir the yeast and sugar into the water in the large bowl. Add the flour and mix to a rough, sticky dough, then cover and leave for 10 minutes so the flour hydrates and the dough becomes easier to knead.

Add the salt and 20 ml of the oil and knead for 8–10 minutes, in the bowl or on the counter, until the dough is smooth, elastic and slightly tacky. It will be softer than ordinary bread dough; resist adding much flour.
Cover the bowl and leave in a warm place for 1–1½ hours, until the dough has doubled in size and is full of bubbles.

Spread the remaining 20 ml of oil over the tray. Tip in the dough and press and stretch it gently towards the corners with oiled fingers. If it keeps springing back, leave it for 10 minutes to relax and try again. Cover and leave for 30–45 minutes, until puffy.
Heat the oven to 230 °C. Whisk the brine ingredients (60 ml oil, 60 ml warm water and the fine salt) in a jug until cloudy.

Dimple the dough: press your fingertips firmly straight down into it all over, right to the tray but without tearing, making deep holes about 2 cm apart. Pour the brine evenly over the top so it pools in the dimples, scatter with the flaky salt and leave for 15–20 minutes more.
Bake on the lower-middle shelf for 20–25 minutes, until the top is golden with paler pools in the dimples and the base is crisp and deep golden when you lift a corner with a spatula.

Slide the focaccia onto a wire rack straight away so the base stays crisp. Cut into 12 squares and eat warm or at room temperature on the day; in Genoa it is even dunked in milky coffee for breakfast.

recipes.storage: Keep wrapped at room temperature for 1 day, or freeze for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Refresh in a 200 °C oven for 5 minutes.
notes: For focaccia with onions or olives, scatter thinly sliced onion or pitted olives over the dough after dimpling.

recipes.name: Pollo alla cacciatora (hunter's-style chicken)
recipes.description: Chicken pieces browned in olive oil and braised slowly with onion, garlic, rosemary, tomatoes and black olives until tender, in a rich, rustic sauce.
equipment: Large heavy casserole or deep frying pan with a lid

steps.t: Pat the chicken pieces dry and season them all over with the salt and pepper. Dry skin browns well; wet skin steams and sticks to the pan.

Heat the oil in the casserole over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken skin-side down in two batches without moving it for 5–6 minutes, until the skin is deep golden and releases easily, then turn and brown the other side for 3 minutes. Set aside on a plate.

Pour off all but about 2 tablespoons of the fat. Lower the heat to medium, add the onion, carrot, celery and a pinch of salt and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring and scraping up the browned bits, until soft and golden. This slow-cooked base is the soffritto that flavours the sauce.

Add the garlic, rosemary and bay and stir for 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the wine, or the vinegar with a splash of the stock, and let it bubble, scraping the base, until reduced by half and the sharp smell has gone, 2–3 minutes.

Add the tomatoes and stock and bring to a simmer. Return the chicken, skin-side up, with any juices; keep the skin above the sauce so it stays savoury rather than soggy. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and simmer gently over low heat for 35–40 minutes, turning the pieces once, until the meat pulls easily from the bone and the thighs read 74 °C next to the bone.
Add the olives for the last 10 minutes. If the sauce is thin, uncover and simmer for 5 minutes more until it coats the back of a spoon. Taste and add salt if needed.
Remove the rosemary stalks and bay leaves, rest the pan off the heat for 5 minutes, scatter with parsley and serve with soft polenta, crusty bread or roast potatoes.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: It tastes even better the next day.
Every region has its own version: peppers are common in the south, mushrooms in the north, and the Roman style uses vinegar, garlic and rosemary with no tomato.

recipes.name: Parmigiana di melanzane (aubergine parmigiana)
recipes.description: Layers of fried aubergine, slow-cooked tomato and basil sauce, mozzarella and Parmigiano, baked until bubbling and left to settle into tender, sliceable layers.

ingredients.name: Sunflower or light olive oil, for shallow frying
Fior di latte mozzarella or provola
ingredients.prep: sliced and drained on kitchen paper

steps.t: Layer the aubergine slices in a colander, sprinkling salt between the layers. Weigh them down with a plate and leave for 30–60 minutes to draw out water. Rinse briefly, squeeze gently and pat completely dry with kitchen paper.

Meanwhile make the sauce: heat the olive oil in the saucepan over medium-low heat and cook the onion for 6–8 minutes until soft and translucent, then add the garlic for 1 minute. Add the passata, salt and a few basil leaves and simmer, partly covered, for 30 minutes, until thick and sweet. It should be thicker than a pasta sauce, or the parmigiana will be watery.

Heat 1 cm of frying oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat to about 175 °C; a slice should sizzle the moment it goes in. Dust the slices lightly in flour, shaking off the excess, and fry in batches for 2–3 minutes per side until deep golden and soft. Drain on kitchen paper and top up the oil as needed.

Heat the oven to 190 °C. Spread a few spoonfuls of sauce over the base of the dish. Add a single layer of aubergine, slightly overlapping, then a thin layer of sauce, some mozzarella, a generous handful of Parmigiano and a few basil leaves.
Repeat to make 3–4 layers, finishing with sauce and a final layer of Parmigiano. Press down gently with a spatula so the layers sit snugly.
Bake for 35–40 minutes, until the edges are bubbling and the top is golden brown in spots.
Leave to rest for at least 30 minutes, ideally an hour, before cutting; it firms up and the flavours settle. Neapolitans often eat it warm or at room temperature, and it is even better the next day.
Cut into squares and serve with crusty bread and a green salad.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate, covered, within 2 hours for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat covered in a 180 °C oven for 20–25 minutes until steaming in the centre, or eat at room temperature.
notes: For a lighter version, brush the slices with oil and bake them at 220 °C for 20 minutes instead of frying.
Mozzarella and Parmigiano are made with animal rennet; use vegetarian alternatives if needed.

recipes.name: Chicken parmigiana
recipes.description: The Italian-American (and Australian pub) favourite: thin chicken cutlets crumbed and fried until crisp, topped with tomato sauce, mozzarella and Parmesan and baked until bubbling.

steps.t: Make the sauce: warm the oil and garlic in the saucepan over medium heat for 1 minute, until fragrant. Add the tomatoes, oregano and salt and simmer for 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick. Tear in the basil.
Lay the chicken cutlets between two sheets of baking paper and pound them with the mallet to an even 1 cm thickness, so they cook evenly and stay juicy. Season both sides with the salt.

Set out three shallow dishes: flour; beaten eggs; breadcrumbs mixed with the 25 g of Parmesan. Dredge each cutlet in flour and shake off the excess, dip it in egg and let the excess drip off, then press it firmly into the crumbs on both sides. Rest on a rack for 10 minutes so the coating sets.

Heat the oven to 220 °C. Heat the frying oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat to about 175 °C; a pinch of crumbs should sizzle at once. Fry the cutlets two at a time for about 3 minutes per side, until deep golden and crisp. Drain on the rack rather than on paper, which steams the underside soft.

Arrange the cutlets on the lined tray. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of sauce over the centre of each, leaving the crumbed edges uncovered so they stay crisp, then top with the mozzarella and the remaining Parmesan.
Bake for 10–12 minutes, until the cheese has melted and browned in spots and the chicken reaches 74 °C in the thickest part.
Rest for 2 minutes, then serve with spaghetti tossed in the leftover sauce, or with chips and a green salad as Australian pubs do.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 200 °C oven for 10–15 minutes until piping hot; the microwave makes the crumb soggy.
notes: Not a dish you will find in Italy, where parmigiana means the aubergine version; it was born in Italian-American kitchens.

recipes.name: Arancine al ragù (Sicilian rice balls)
recipes.description: Palermo's golden street food: saffron rice wrapped around a slow-cooked beef and pea ragù with a cube of melting cheese, crumbed and deep-fried until crisp. Makes 12 large arancine.

steps.t: Cook the rice: bring the water and salt to the boil, add the rice and the saffron with its soaking water, cover and cook over very low heat for 15–18 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the water is absorbed and the rice is tender. Unlike risotto, it should end up dry, not creamy.

Off the heat, stir in the butter and cheese. Spread the rice on the large tray in an even layer, cover with a cloth and leave to cool completely, at least 2 hours or overnight in the fridge. Cold, sticky rice is what holds the shape.

Make the ragù: heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion and carrot for 8 minutes until soft. Raise the heat, add the beef and break it up, browning it for 5–6 minutes until no pink remains. Add the wine, if using, and let it bubble away.

Stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute, then add the passata, salt, pepper and a splash of water. Simmer gently for 25–30 minutes, adding the peas for the last 5, until the ragù is very thick and almost dry; a wet ragù leaks through the rice. Leave to cool completely.

Shape the arancine with wet hands: take a portion of rice the size of a small orange (about 110 g), flatten it into a cup in your palm, add a heaped tablespoon of ragù and a cube of cheese, then close the rice around the filling, adding a little more rice to seal any gaps. Press firmly into a ball. Repeat to make about 12.

Whisk the flour and cold water into a smooth batter like thick cream. Roll each ball in the batter, then in the breadcrumbs, pressing so the coating covers it completely. Chill for 30 minutes to firm up.

Heat the oil in the deep pan (no more than one-third full) to 175 °C. Fry 3 arancine at a time, turning gently, for 4–5 minutes, until deep golden brown and hot right through (74 °C in the centre). Keep the oil temperature steady between batches and drain on a rack.
Rest for 5 minutes before eating, because the cheese centre is molten. Eat warm, in the hand, as they do in Palermo.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate fried arancine within 2 hours and eat within 2 days. Uncooked, crumbed arancine freeze well for 1 month; fry from frozen at 160 °C for 8–10 minutes.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 200 °C oven for 15–20 minutes until piping hot in the centre.
notes: In Palermo they are arancine and round; in Catania, arancini and cone-shaped.
The other classic filling, al burro, is béchamel, mozzarella and diced ham.

recipes.name: Caponata (Sicilian sweet-and-sour aubergine)
recipes.description: Fried aubergine folded into a sweet-and-sour stew of celery, onion, tomato, green olives and capers, sharpened with vinegar and sugar and best eaten at room temperature.

steps.t: Toss the aubergine with the salt in a colander and leave for 30 minutes to draw out water, then pat dry with kitchen paper. This helps it fry crisp instead of soaking up oil.
Heat 120 ml of the oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the aubergine in batches, turning, until golden on all sides and tender, 6–8 minutes per batch. Drain on kitchen paper.

Heat the remaining oil in the sauté pan over medium heat. Fry the celery for 5 minutes until lightly golden but still crunchy and lift it out. Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes until soft and translucent.
Add the tomatoes and simmer for 10 minutes until thick, then stir in the olives, capers and the celery and cook for 3 minutes.

Stir the sugar into the vinegar, pour it into the pan and simmer for 2–3 minutes, until the sharp smell of vinegar softens. The agrodolce (sweet-and-sour) balance should be lively but not harsh; taste and adjust with a little more sugar or vinegar.

Gently fold in the aubergine and heat through for 2 minutes. Off the heat, add the torn basil, and the pine nuts and raisins if using. Leave to cool for at least an hour before serving; caponata is eaten at room temperature and is better the next day.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate in a covered container for up to 5 days; bring back to room temperature before serving.
notes: Serve as an antipasto with bread, alongside grilled fish, or as a side dish. Pine nuts and raisins are typical of Palermo.

recipes.name: Ribollita (Tuscan bread and bean soup)
recipes.description: Tuscany's thick winter soup of cannellini beans, cavolo nero, cabbage and vegetables, thickened with stale bread and traditionally reheated — 'reboiled' — the next day.

ingredients.name: Cannellini beans, drained (or 250 g dried, soaked and cooked)
Stale country bread (Tuscan bread is unsalted)
Extra virgin olive oil, to finish

steps.t: Heat 4 tablespoons of oil in the pot over medium-low heat. Add the onion, carrot, celery and a pinch of salt and cook gently for 12–15 minutes, stirring often, until soft and sweet but not browned. This slow base gives the soup its depth.
Add the garlic and thyme and stir for 1 minute, then add the tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes until slightly thickened.

Mash or blend one can of the beans with a ladle of the stock to a smooth purée; it thickens the soup. Add it to the pot with the whole beans, the remaining stock, potato, cavolo nero, cabbage, salt and the Parmesan rind, if using. Bring to the boil, then simmer, partly covered, for 45 minutes until the cabbage is very soft and the soup is thick.

Fish out the thyme stalks and the rind. Lay half the bread in the base of a clean pot or deep ovenproof dish, ladle over half the soup, then add the rest of the bread and soup. Leave for 15 minutes so the bread soaks up the broth.

For true ribollita, cool it, refrigerate overnight and next day reheat slowly, stirring, until the bread breaks down and the soup is thick enough for a spoon to stand in it. To eat it the same day, simmer for 10 minutes more, stirring, until the bread dissolves.
Season with the pepper and more salt if needed. Serve in warm bowls with a generous thread of olive oil on top; in Florence it comes with sliced raw red onion on the side.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Ribollita improves on the second and third day.
Leave out the Parmesan rind for a vegan soup.

recipes.name: Insalata caprese (tomato, mozzarella and basil salad)
recipes.description: Capri's summer salad in the colours of the Italian flag: ripe tomatoes and fresh mozzarella sliced and layered with basil, dressed simply with salt and good olive oil.

ingredients.name: Fresh mozzarella (buffalo or fior di latte)

steps.t: Take the tomatoes and mozzarella out of the fridge 30 minutes before serving, because cold dulls their flavour. Choose the ripest, heaviest tomatoes you can find: with so few ingredients there is nowhere to hide.

Slice the tomatoes 1 cm thick with the serrated knife. Slice the mozzarella to the same thickness, or tear it for a softer look, and pat it with kitchen paper so its milk doesn't water down the dressing.
Arrange alternating, overlapping slices of tomato and mozzarella on the platter, tucking a basil leaf between each.

Just before serving, season with the flaky salt (and a pinch of oregano if you like) and pour over the olive oil in a thin stream. Serve at once with crusty bread to mop up the juices. In Campania there is no vinegar or balsamic.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within an hour of making; don't refrigerate the dressed salad.

recipes.name: Gnocchi di patate al burro e salvia (potato gnocchi with sage butter)
recipes.description: Light, pillowy potato dumplings made from baked floury potatoes and just enough flour, tossed in nutty browned butter with crisp sage leaves and Parmigiano.

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (russet or Maris Piper), similar size

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Prick the potatoes and bake them on the tray for 50–60 minutes, until tender all the way through. Baking rather than boiling keeps them dry, so you need less flour, which is the secret of light gnocchi.
While the potatoes are still hot, halve them, scoop out the flesh and pass it through the ricer onto a floured work surface in an even layer. Leave for 5 minutes so the steam escapes.

Sprinkle over the salt and most of the flour, add the egg and bring everything together with your fingertips or a dough scraper. Knead gently for 1–2 minutes, just until you have a soft, smooth dough that no longer sticks; overworking makes gnocchi tough and gummy. Drop a small piece into simmering salted water: if it falls apart, work in a little more flour.

Cut the dough into 6 pieces and roll each into a rope about 2 cm thick on the floured surface. Cut into 2 cm lengths, then roll each piece over the back of a fork with your thumb to make ridges and a dimple that hold the sauce. Spread them out on a floured tray so they don't touch.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a gentle boil. Meanwhile melt the butter in the frying pan over medium heat with the sage. Cook for 3–4 minutes until the butter foams, turns hazelnut brown and smells nutty and the sage is crisp, then take it off the heat; browned butter burns quickly.
Cook the gnocchi in 2–3 batches. They sink, then rise to the surface after 1½–2 minutes; let them bob for 30 seconds more, then lift them out with the slotted spoon straight into the butter pan.
Add 2 tablespoons of the cooking water to the pan and toss gently over low heat for 30 seconds so the butter glazes the gnocchi. Serve topped with the crisp sage, Parmigiano and black pepper.

recipes.storage: Uncooked gnocchi freeze well: freeze on the tray, then bag and cook from frozen (allow 1 extra minute). Cooked gnocchi are best eaten fresh; refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Pan-fry leftovers in a little butter until golden and hot through.
notes: Some Venetian cooks leave out the egg; the dough is more delicate but even lighter.

recipes.name: Panna cotta with raspberry sauce
recipes.description: Piedmont's 'cooked cream': sweetened vanilla cream set with just enough gelatine to hold a gentle wobble, served chilled with a sharp raspberry sauce.
equipment: Six 125 ml moulds, ramekins or glasses

steps.t: Sprinkle the gelatine over the cold milk in the small bowl (or soak the leaves in cold water) and leave for 5–10 minutes until spongy. This 'blooming' lets it dissolve smoothly later.

Heat the cream and sugar (with the split vanilla pod and its scraped seeds, if using) in the saucepan over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves and the cream is steaming with small bubbles at the edge, about 5 minutes. Don't let it boil hard.

Take the pan off the heat, add the gelatine and milk (or the squeezed-out leaves) and stir for about a minute until completely dissolved, with no grains left on the spoon. Stir in the vanilla extract and strain into a jug.

Leave to cool for 10 minutes, stirring now and then so the vanilla seeds don't sink, then pour into the moulds (lightly oiled if you plan to turn them out). Cover and chill for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, until set but still wobbly.
Make the sauce: simmer the raspberries, sugar and lemon juice in a small pan for about 5 minutes until the berries collapse. Press through the sieve to remove the seeds and leave to cool.

To serve, dip each mould in hot water for 5–10 seconds, run a thin knife around the edge and turn out onto a plate with a gentle shake. Spoon the sauce around, or simply pour it over panna cotta set in glasses.

recipes.storage: @chilled
notes: Gelatine is made from animal collagen. For a vegetarian version, boil the cream with about 1 tsp agar-agar powder for 2 minutes instead.

recipes.name: Risotto alla milanese (saffron risotto)
recipes.description: Milan's golden risotto: short-grain rice toasted in butter, cooked slowly with hot stock and saffron, and finished with cold butter and Parmigiano until creamy and flowing.

ingredients.name: Butter
ingredients.prep: 30 g to start; 30 g cold and diced to finish

steps.t: Bring the stock to a bare simmer and keep it hot over low heat beside the risotto pan; cold stock stalls the rice. Crumble the saffron into a cup with a small ladle of hot stock and leave it to steep while you start the rice.
Melt 30 g of the butter in the wide pan over medium-low heat and cook the onion gently for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent but not coloured.
Raise the heat to medium, add the rice and stir for about 2 minutes, until the grains are hot, glossy and translucent at the edges. This toasting (tostatura) helps them release their starch slowly.

Pour in the wine, if using, and stir until it has evaporated. Add a ladle of hot stock and stir until it is almost absorbed, then add the next, keeping the rice at a lively simmer. Continue for 16–18 minutes, stirring often.
About halfway through, stir in the saffron and its liquid; the rice turns a deep golden yellow.

When the rice is tender with a slight bite in the centre and the risotto is loose enough to flow like a slow wave (all'onda), take the pan off the heat. Add the cold diced butter and the Parmigiano and beat hard with the wooden spoon for 30 seconds until creamy and glossy; this is the mantecatura. Cover and rest for 2 minutes.
Taste for salt and serve at once on warm plates, tapping the underside so the risotto spreads out. In Milan it is served alone or with ossobuco.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; refrigerate leftovers within 1 hour and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with a splash of stock until steaming hot, or press into a thin cake and fry in butter until crisp on both sides (risotto al salto).
notes: Milanese cooks traditionally add a spoonful of beef bone marrow with the onion for extra richness.
Use vegetable stock for a vegetarian risotto; Parmigiano is made with animal rennet.

recipes.name: Ratatouille
recipes.description: Provence's summer vegetable stew: aubergine, courgettes, peppers and onions cooked separately in olive oil, then simmered together with tomatoes, garlic and herbs until soft and melded.
equipment: Large heavy casserole with a lid

ingredients.name: Courgettes (2–3)
ingredients.prep: halved lengthways and cut into 1.5 cm slices

ingredients.name: Dried thyme or herbes de Provence

steps.t: Peel the tomatoes: cut a small cross in the base of each, plunge into boiling water for 30 seconds, then into cold water, and the skins will slip off. Halve them, squeeze out the seeds and chop the flesh.

Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the aubergine with a pinch of salt, stirring, for 8–10 minutes until golden and soft. Tip into the casserole. Cooking each vegetable separately is the Niçoise way: each keeps its own flavour and texture.

Add another tablespoon of oil and fry the courgettes for 5–6 minutes until lightly golden but still holding their shape; add them to the casserole. Fry the peppers in a little more oil for 6–8 minutes until soft and lightly charred at the edges, and add those too.

Lower the heat to medium, add 2 tablespoons of oil and the onions with a pinch of salt and cook for 10 minutes until soft and golden. Add the garlic for 1 minute, then the tomatoes, thyme and bay, and cook for 10 minutes until saucy.

Tip the tomato mixture into the casserole, stir gently and season with the salt and pepper. Cover and simmer over low heat for 30–40 minutes, stirring gently once or twice, until all the vegetables are meltingly soft and the juices have thickened. Uncover for the last 10 minutes if it looks watery.

Take off the heat, remove the bay leaf and stir in the basil and the remaining oil. Leave to rest for at least 15 minutes; ratatouille is best warm or at room temperature, and better still the next day.
Serve as a main course with crusty bread, rice or a fried egg on top, or as a side dish with grilled fish or meat.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate in a covered container for up to 4 days, or freeze for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Quiche aux poireaux (leek quiche)
recipes.description: A crisp, buttery shortcrust case filled with leeks melted slowly in butter and a silky custard of eggs, cream and Gruyère, baked until just set and golden.
equipment: 23 cm loose-bottomed tart tin, 3–4 cm deep
Baking paper and baking beans or dry rice

ingredients.name: Leeks (about 4 medium), trimmed
ingredients.prep: halved lengthways, washed and sliced 1 cm thick

steps.t: Make the pastry: rub the butter into the flour and salt with your fingertips until it looks like fine breadcrumbs, working quickly so the butter stays cold. Mix the yolk with 2 tablespoons of the iced water, add it and bring the dough together with a knife, adding the rest of the water a teaspoon at a time only if it is dry. Don't knead; press it into a disc, wrap and chill for 30 minutes.

Roll the pastry out on a floured surface to 3 mm thick and about 30 cm across. Line the tin, pressing it into the corners and leaving a little overhang. Prick the base with a fork and chill for 15 minutes so it doesn't shrink in the oven.

Heat the oven to 190 °C with a baking tray inside. Line the pastry with baking paper, fill with beans and bake on the hot tray for 15 minutes; remove the paper and beans and bake for 8–10 minutes more until the base is dry and pale golden. Blind baking keeps the base crisp under the wet filling. Trim the overhang and lower the oven to 170 °C.

Meanwhile melt the butter in the frying pan over medium-low heat, add the leeks and salt, cover and sweat for 15–20 minutes, stirring now and then, until very soft and sweet but not browned. Uncover for the last few minutes to drive off their liquid; wet leeks make a watery quiche. Leave to cool slightly.
Whisk the eggs, yolk, cream, milk, nutmeg and pepper until smooth, without beating in lots of air.
Spread the leeks over the pastry and scatter over the Gruyère. Set the tin on the hot tray in the oven and pour in the custard almost to the top; filling it in the oven avoids spills.
Bake at 170 °C for 30–35 minutes, until golden and set with a slight wobble in the centre; it keeps setting as it cools. A knife pushed in 3 cm from the edge should come out clean.
Cool in the tin for 20 minutes before unmoulding and slicing. Serve warm or at room temperature with a green salad and a sharp vinaigrette.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Eat cold or at room temperature, or warm slices in a 160 °C oven for 15 minutes.
notes: About 300 g of ready-made shortcrust pastry saves time.
Gruyère is usually made with animal rennet.

recipes.name: Soupe à l'oignon gratinée (French onion soup)
recipes.description: Onions cooked slowly in butter until deep brown and jammy, simmered in beef stock with thyme, then topped with toasted baguette and Gruyère and grilled until bubbling.

steps.t: Melt the butter with the oil in the heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onions and salt and stir to coat, then cover and cook for 10 minutes until wilted and juicy.

Uncover, add the sugar and cook over medium-low heat for 45–60 minutes, stirring every few minutes and scraping the base, until the onions are a deep mahogany brown, jammy and sweet. If they catch, add a splash of water and scrape up the brown film, which is pure flavour. High heat burns them before they caramelise, so be patient.
Add the garlic and stir for 1 minute, then sprinkle over the flour and stir for 2 minutes to cook out its raw taste.

Pour in the wine, if using, and bubble for 2 minutes while scraping the base; otherwise deglaze with a ladle of stock and the vinegar. Add the remaining stock, thyme and bay, and simmer, partly covered, for 25–30 minutes. Season with pepper and more salt if needed.
Meanwhile toast the baguette slices on the baking tray in a 200 °C oven for 8–10 minutes, until dry and crisp right through; crisp bread holds up in the soup instead of turning to mush.
Heat the grill to high. Remove the thyme and bay. Set the ovenproof bowls on a tray, ladle in the hot soup, float two toasts in each and cover generously with Gruyère, letting it overhang the rim.
Grill for 3–5 minutes, until the cheese is melted, bubbling and browned in spots. Serve at once, warning everyone that the bowls are scalding.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the soup without bread and cheese for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: The deeper the onions' colour, the richer the soup; a good homemade stock makes the biggest difference.

recipes.name: Crêpes (thin French pancakes with sugar and lemon)
recipes.description: Thin, lacy wheat-flour crêpes cooked in a hot buttered pan and served the Breton way, folded with butter and sugar and a squeeze of lemon, or with jam or honey. Makes about 12.
equipment: 24–26 cm crêpe pan or non-stick frying pan

steps.t: Whisk the flour, salt and sugar in the bowl and make a well in the centre. Add the eggs and a splash of the milk and whisk from the middle outwards, gradually drawing in the flour and adding milk a little at a time. Making a smooth, thick paste first and then thinning it is the way to avoid lumps.

Whisk in the remaining milk and the melted butter until the batter is as thin as single cream. If you have time, rest it for 30 minutes so the flour hydrates and the crêpes are more tender; otherwise use it straight away. Strain it if any lumps remain.
Heat the pan over medium-high heat until a drop of water dances and evaporates at once. Wipe it with a piece of kitchen paper dipped in the butter for the pan.
Lift the pan off the heat, pour in a small ladle (about 50 ml) of batter and immediately tilt and rotate the pan so it covers the base in a thin, even layer. Pour any excess back into the bowl.

Cook for about 1 minute, until the edges lift and turn lacy brown and the underside is golden. Loosen with the spatula, flip and cook for 30 seconds more. The first crêpe is usually a tester; adjust the heat or thin the batter with a little milk if needed.
Stack the crêpes on a warm plate under a clean cloth while you cook the rest, buttering the pan every 2–3 crêpes.
Serve warm: brush each crêpe with a little butter, sprinkle with sugar and a squeeze of lemon and fold into quarters, or spread with jam or honey.

recipes.storage: Stack cooled crêpes between sheets of baking paper, wrap and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a dry pan for 20 seconds on each side.

recipes.name: Galette complète with spinach (buckwheat crêpe with egg and cheese)
recipes.description: Brittany's savoury buckwheat galette, crisp and nutty, folded around melted Emmental, sautéed spinach and an egg with a soft yolk. This version uses spinach in place of the usual ham.
equipment: Large crêpe pan or 28 cm non-stick frying pan

ingredients.name: Salted butter, melted, for the pan

steps.t: Make the batter: whisk the buckwheat flour and salt in the bowl, make a well, add the egg and half the water and beat to a thick, smooth paste for 2–3 minutes; Breton cooks beat it by hand to give the batter body. Whisk in the rest of the water until it is like thin cream. Cover and rest for at least 1 hour, or overnight in the fridge. It thickens as it rests, so thin it with a splash of water if needed.
Melt the 10 g of butter in the small frying pan, add the spinach and toss for 2 minutes until just wilted. Tip into a sieve, press out the liquid and season with pepper.

Heat the large pan over medium-high heat until very hot and brush it with melted butter. Pour in a ladle (about 80 ml) of batter and swirl or spread it quickly into a thin, even layer covering the pan. Cook for 1–2 minutes, until the edges are crisp and lift easily and the surface looks dry.

Turn the galette over for 20 seconds and then back again, and lower the heat to medium. Crack an egg into the centre and spread the white gently with the back of a spoon so it cooks evenly, keeping the yolk whole. Scatter cheese around the yolk and add a sixth of the spinach.
Cook for 2–3 minutes, covering the pan with a lid for the last minute, until the white is set and the cheese has melted. Brush the edges with a little butter.
Fold the four sides in towards the centre to make a square, leaving the yolk showing through the window in the middle. Slide onto a warm plate and keep warm in a low oven while you cook the rest.
Serve at once with a green salad; in Brittany a bowl of cider is traditional, and alcohol-free cider works well.

recipes.storage: Galettes are best eaten straight away. Leftover batter keeps for 2 days in the fridge.
recipes.reheating: Reheat plain galettes in a dry pan for 30 seconds, then fill and cook to order.
notes: Buckwheat is naturally gluten-free; check that the flour is not milled with wheat if that matters to you.
The classic complète has a slice of ham with the cheese and egg.

recipes.name: Salade niçoise
recipes.description: A main-course salad from Nice: crisp lettuce, ripe tomatoes, green beans, new potatoes and jammy eggs, topped with tuna, anchovies and black olives and dressed with a mustardy vinaigrette.

steps.t: Put the potatoes in the saucepan, cover with cold salted water, bring to the boil and simmer for 12–15 minutes until a knife slips through easily. Add the green beans for the last 3–4 minutes, until bright green and just tender. Drain both and spread out to cool slightly.
Meanwhile lower the eggs into a small pan of simmering water and cook for 7–8 minutes for jammy yolks. Cool them in cold water for 2 minutes, then peel and quarter.
Shake the oil, vinegar, mustard, garlic, salt and pepper in the jar until thick and emulsified. Toss the still-warm potatoes and beans with a third of the dressing; warm potatoes soak it up.

Line the platter with lettuce. Arrange the tomatoes, pepper, spring onions, potatoes and beans in groups, then top with chunks of tuna, the eggs, anchovies and olives. Drizzle over the rest of the dressing, scatter with torn basil and serve straight away with crusty bread.

recipes.storage: Best assembled just before eating. Undressed components keep for 2 days in the fridge.
notes: Niçois purists use only raw vegetables, with no potatoes or cooked beans; this is the more common home version.

recipes.name: Tarte Tatin (upside-down caramelised apple tart)
recipes.description: Apples cooked in buttery caramel until deep amber, covered with puff pastry and baked, then turned out so the glossy caramelised fruit sits on top of crisp pastry.
equipment: 24 cm heavy ovenproof frying pan or tarte Tatin dish
Serving plate larger than the pan

ingredients.name: Firm apples that hold their shape (about 7; Golden Delicious, Cox or Braeburn)
Crème fraîche or vanilla ice cream, to serve

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Toss the apple quarters with the lemon juice. Roll the pastry into a circle 2–3 cm wider than the pan, prick it all over with a fork and chill it on a plate while you make the caramel.

Scatter the sugar evenly over the base of the pan and set it over medium heat. Let it melt without stirring, swirling the pan once the edges turn liquid, until it is all melted and a deep amber, the colour of a conker, 6–8 minutes. Watch closely: amber turns to burnt in seconds.
Take the pan off the heat and add the butter; it will foam furiously. Swirl or stir until the caramel is smooth.

Arrange the apple quarters upright, rounded side down, packed tightly in circles; they shrink as they cook, so squeeze in more than seems possible. Return to medium-low heat and cook for 15–20 minutes, basting with the caramel, until the apples are half soft (a skewer meets slight resistance) and the caramel is thick and darker.
Lay the cold pastry over the apples and tuck the edges down inside the pan with a spoon, taking care with the hot caramel. Cut 2–3 small slits for steam.
Bake for 25–30 minutes, until the pastry is puffed and deep golden.

Rest for 5 minutes, no longer, or the caramel will set and stick. Run a knife round the edge, put the serving plate on top and, wearing oven gloves, turn it over in one swift, confident movement. Lift off the pan and put back any apples that stuck.
Serve warm, in wedges, with crème fraîche or vanilla ice cream.

recipes.storage: Keep at room temperature for up to 1 day, or refrigerate for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm slices in a 160 °C oven for 10 minutes.

recipes.name: Crème brûlée
recipes.description: A rich, silky vanilla custard of cream and egg yolks baked gently in a water bath, chilled, then topped with sugar caramelised into a thin, glassy crust that cracks under the spoon.
equipment: Kitchen blowtorch or very hot grill

ingredients.name: Vanilla pod, split (or 1 tsp vanilla extract)
Caster or demerara sugar, for the topping

steps.t: Heat the oven to 150 °C. Stand the ramekins in the roasting tin and boil a kettle of water.
Heat the cream, milk and split vanilla pod (with its seeds scraped in) in the saucepan until steaming, with small bubbles at the edge. Take off the heat, cover and leave to infuse for 10 minutes.
Whisk the yolks and the 80 g of sugar in the bowl until pale and smooth. Just combine them; beating in lots of air leaves bubbles on the finished custard.

Remove the vanilla pod and bring the cream back to steaming. Pour it onto the yolks in a thin stream, whisking all the time, so the yolks warm gradually without scrambling; this is called tempering. Strain into a jug and skim off any foam.

Pour the custard into the ramekins and add hot water to the tin to come halfway up their sides. Bake for 30–40 minutes, until set at the edges with a gentle wobble in the centre, like a set jelly, when you nudge the tin (about 80 °C in the centre).
Lift the ramekins out of the water, leave to cool, then chill for at least 3 hours or overnight.

Just before serving, blot any moisture from the surface and sprinkle each custard with an even, thin layer of sugar (about 2 teaspoons). Caramelise with the blowtorch, keeping it moving, until the sugar melts, bubbles and turns deep amber, or slide under a very hot grill for 2–3 minutes. Leave for 2 minutes so the caramel hardens into glass, then serve.

recipes.storage: Keep the baked custards covered in the fridge for up to 3 days; caramelise the tops just before serving.
notes: Save the egg whites for meringues or an omelette; they keep 4 days in the fridge or 3 months frozen.

recipes.name: Gratin dauphinois (creamy baked potatoes)
recipes.description: Thinly sliced potatoes simmered in garlic-scented milk and cream, then baked slowly until meltingly tender with a golden, bubbling top. The Dauphiné original has no cheese.

ingredients.name: Waxy or all-purpose potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and sliced 3 mm thick; don't rinse

steps.t: Heat the oven to 160 °C. Rub the inside of the dish with the cut garlic clove, then butter it generously.
Slice the potatoes thinly and evenly; a mandoline makes this quick. Don't rinse the slices: their surface starch thickens the cream.

Put the potatoes, milk, cream, crushed garlic, bay, salt, nutmeg and pepper in the saucepan and bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring carefully with a spatula so the slices don't stick. Simmer for 8–10 minutes, until the liquid thickens and the potatoes begin to soften. Taste the liquid: it should be well seasoned.
Remove the bay leaf and tip everything into the dish, spreading the slices flat and pressing them down so they are just covered by the liquid.

Bake for 60–75 minutes, until the top is deep golden in patches, the cream is bubbling and thick and a knife slides through the potatoes with no resistance. Cover loosely with foil if it browns too quickly.
Rest for 10–15 minutes before serving so the cream settles and the gratin slices cleanly. Serve with roast chicken or lamb, or with a green salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat, covered, in a 170 °C oven for 20–25 minutes until steaming hot.
notes: Many cooks add grated Gruyère on top; that is closer to a gratin savoyard, and very good.

recipes.name: Paella valenciana (chicken and bean paella)
recipes.description: The original paella from the rice fields around Valencia: chicken browned slowly in olive oil with flat green beans and butter beans, then cooked with tomato, saffron and rosemary into a thin layer of rice with a crisp, caramelised base.
equipment: Paella pan, 38–40 cm (or the widest frying pan you have)
Large burner, two burners or a barbecue

ingredients.name: Chicken thighs and drumsticks, bone-in, skinless
Flat green beans (ferraura) or runner beans
ingredients.prep: trimmed and cut into 4 cm pieces

ingredients.name: Cooked butter beans (garrofó) or large white beans
Bomba or other Spanish paella rice

steps.t: Set the pan level over the burner or barbecue. Heat the oil over medium-high heat, add the chicken seasoned with 1 teaspoon of the salt in a single layer and brown it slowly, turning, for 15–20 minutes until deep golden all over. This browning, in the paella pan itself, is the flavour base of the dish.
Push the chicken to the edges, put the green beans in the centre and fry for 4–5 minutes until blistered in places. Stir in the butter beans.

Clear a space in the centre, add the garlic for 30 seconds, then the grated tomato, and cook for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and turns jammy. This is the sofrito. Stir in the paprika for just 10 seconds; it burns quickly.

Immediately pour in the water, add the saffron and the remaining salt and bring to the boil. Simmer for 20 minutes to make a flavourful broth while the chicken finishes cooking. Taste it: it should be slightly too salty, because the rice absorbs salt. Top up with water if it has dropped well below the rivets of the handles.

Scatter the rice evenly over the pan and spread it with a spoon so it is evenly distributed and submerged. From now on, do not stir. Cook over high heat for 8–10 minutes, moving the pan over the flame so it cooks evenly, until the rice rises to the surface and the broth has reduced.

Lay the rosemary on top, lower the heat to medium-low and cook for 8–10 minutes more, until the liquid is absorbed and the rice is tender with a slight bite. Small craters appear on the surface as the last liquid evaporates.
For the socarrat, the prized crisp base, raise the heat for the final 1–2 minutes. Listen for a gentle crackling and smell for a toasty (not burnt) aroma, then take the pan off the heat.
Cover with a clean tea towel and rest for 5 minutes. Serve from the pan at the table, scraping up the crisp bits from the base.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate within 1 hour and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Valencia's original also has rabbit, and sometimes snails; use half chicken and half rabbit if you can get it.
Garrofó are large, flat Valencian lima beans; canned butter beans are the closest substitute.

recipes.name: Paella de marisco (seafood paella)
recipes.description: A coastal paella cooked in a rich prawn-shell stock with squid, prawns and mussels, a sofrito of red pepper, garlic and tomato, saffron and paprika, finished with a crisp socarrat.

ingredients.name: Raw prawns, peeled weight (about 12 large shell-on prawns)
ingredients.prep: peeled; keep the heads and shells

ingredients.name: Squid, cleaned
ingredients.prep: cut into rings; tentacles kept whole

ingredients.name: Bomba or other Spanish paella rice

steps.t: Make a quick shellfish stock: heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in the saucepan over high heat and fry the prawn heads and shells for 3–4 minutes, pressing the heads to release their juices, until bright red. Add the fish stock, simmer for 15 minutes, then strain and keep hot.
Put the mussels and water in the lidded pan, cover and steam over high heat for 3–4 minutes, shaking the pan, until they open. Discard any that stay closed. Strain the cooking liquid into the stock.

Heat the remaining oil in the paella pan over medium-high heat. Sear the prawns for 1 minute per side until just pink and lift them out; they will finish cooking on the rice. Add the squid and cook for 3 minutes until opaque and lightly coloured.
Add the red pepper and cook for 5 minutes until soft, then the garlic for 1 minute and the grated tomato for about 5 minutes, until dark and jammy. Stir in the paprika for 10 seconds.

Add the rice and stir for 1 minute to coat it in the sofrito. Pour in 1.2 litres of the hot stock with the saffron and salt, stir once to spread the rice evenly and taste the broth; it should be well seasoned. Do not stir again. Cook over high heat for 10 minutes, moving the pan over the flame.

Lower the heat to medium-low and cook for about 8 minutes more. When the liquid is nearly absorbed, nestle the prawns and mussels into the surface and cook for 2–3 minutes, until the rice is tender and the prawns are cooked through. Sprinkle over a little more stock if the rice is still hard.

Raise the heat for the last 1–2 minutes until you hear crackling and smell toasting rice: that is the socarrat forming. Cover with a tea towel and rest for 5 minutes, then scatter with parsley and serve with lemon wedges.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate within 1 hour and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Arroz negro, coloured with squid ink, and arroz a banda, cooked in a rich fish stock, are close relatives made the same way.

recipes.name: Tortilla de patatas (Spanish potato omelette)
recipes.description: Spain's thick potato and onion omelette: potatoes and onion poached slowly in olive oil until tender, folded into beaten eggs and cooked gently into a golden cake that is just set, or still juicy, in the middle.
equipment: Large flat plate or lid for flipping

ingredients.name: Olive oil (most is drained off and can be reused)
Waxy potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled, quartered lengthways and thinly sliced

steps.t: Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat; a slice of potato should bubble gently rather than fry hard. Add the potatoes and onion with 1 teaspoon of the salt; they should be just covered. Cook for 20–25 minutes, turning them gently now and then and lowering the heat if they start to brown, until completely tender and breaking when pressed. You are poaching them in oil, not frying them.
Tip the potatoes and onion into the sieve over a bowl to drain, keeping the oil (strain it later to reuse). Leave to cool for 5 minutes.

Beat the eggs with the remaining salt in the large bowl just until combined. Add the warm potatoes and onion, pressing lightly so a few slices break, and leave for 10 minutes so the potatoes soak up the egg; this is what makes a tortilla hold together.

Wipe out the pan, add 2 tablespoons of the drained oil and heat over medium-high heat. Pour in the mixture and spread it evenly, shaking the pan and running a spatula around the edge to shape the sides. Lower the heat to medium-low and cook for 4–5 minutes, until the underside is golden and the edges are set but the top is still runny.

To flip, put the plate on top of the pan, hold it firmly with one hand and turn the pan over in one quick, confident movement. Add a teaspoon of oil to the pan and slide the tortilla back in, uncooked side down, tucking in the edges with the spatula.
Cook for 2 minutes more for a juicy centre, as many Spanish bars serve it, or about 4 minutes for a fully set one; the centre feels firm when pressed once it is set. Slide onto a plate.
Rest for at least 5 minutes before cutting into wedges. Eat warm or at room temperature with bread and a tomato salad, or cut into cubes as a tapa.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Best at room temperature; or warm slices in a low oven for 10 minutes.
notes: Whether to add onion divides Spain; leave it out for a tortilla sin cebolla.

recipes.name: Gazpacho andaluz (chilled tomato soup)
recipes.description: Andalusia's cold summer soup: ripe tomatoes, cucumber, green pepper, garlic and a little bread blended with olive oil and sherry vinegar until smooth and refreshing.

ingredients.name: Green pepper (Italian frying pepper if possible)
Ice-cold water or a handful of ice cubes

steps.t: Use the ripest, reddest tomatoes you can find; pale ones give a pink, watery soup. Core and chop them, and chop the cucumber, pepper and garlic so the blender can work evenly.
Soak the bread in a little water for 5 minutes, then squeeze it out. The bread gives gazpacho its body and helps the oil emulsify.
Put the tomatoes, cucumber, pepper, garlic, bread, vinegar and salt in the blender and blend on high for 1–2 minutes, until completely smooth.
With the motor running, pour in the oil in a slow, steady stream. The soup turns paler orange and creamy as the oil emulsifies. Add the cold water (or ice) to loosen it to a drinkable consistency.
Taste and adjust with more salt or vinegar; it should taste bright and balanced. For a silky finish, press it through a fine sieve.
Chill for at least an hour, or blend in a few ice cubes and serve straight away. Serve in chilled glasses or bowls topped with the diced cucumber and onion and a few drops of olive oil.

recipes.storage: Keeps covered in the fridge for up to 3 days; stir before serving.
notes: Gazpacho is drunk from a glass in Andalusian homes through the summer.

recipes.name: Patatas bravas
recipes.description: Madrid's favourite tapa: rough chunks of potato fried until crisp and golden, served hot under a smoky, spicy paprika sauce.

ingredients.name: Floury or all-purpose potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 3 cm irregular chunks

ingredients.name: Olive or sunflower oil, for frying
Sweet smoked paprika (pimentón de la Vera)

steps.t: Put the potatoes in a saucepan of cold salted water, bring to the boil and simmer for 5–6 minutes, until the edges are just soft but the centres still firm. Drain, shake in the colander to rough up the edges and spread on a tray to steam dry for 10 minutes. Dry, rough surfaces fry up crunchy.

Make the salsa brava: warm the oil and garlic in the small pan over medium-low heat for 1 minute, stir in the flour for 1 minute, then take the pan off the heat and stir in both paprikas, which scorch easily. Whisk in the stock a little at a time until smooth and simmer for 5 minutes until thick like ketchup. Add the vinegar and salt, and blend smooth if you like.

Heat the frying oil in the deep pan (no more than one-third full) to 180 °C. Fry the potatoes in two batches for 8–10 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper and salt immediately.
Pile the potatoes onto a plate, spoon over the hot sauce as they do in Madrid, and serve with cocktail sticks. In Catalonia a spoonful of garlicky alioli goes on as well.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. The sauce keeps for 5 days in the fridge.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp leftover potatoes in a 220 °C oven for 10 minutes and warm the sauce separately.

recipes.name: Gambas al ajillo (garlic prawns)
recipes.description: Sizzling prawns cooked in plenty of olive oil with sliced garlic and dried chilli, served bubbling in the dish with bread to mop up the oil.
equipment: Terracotta cazuela or small heavy frying pan

ingredients.name: Raw prawns, peeled and deveined
ingredients.prep: tails left on if you like

ingredients.name: Dried guindilla or other small dried chillies

steps.t: Pat the prawns very dry with kitchen paper and season with the salt; dry prawns sizzle in the oil instead of stewing.
Put the oil and garlic in the cazuela over medium-low heat and warm gently for 3–4 minutes, until the garlic sizzles and is just turning pale gold. Add the chillies for 30 seconds.

Raise the heat to medium-high and add the prawns in a single layer. Cook for 1–2 minutes per side, turning once, until pink, curled and just opaque all the way through; overcooked prawns turn rubbery.
Take off the heat, scatter with parsley and serve immediately, still sizzling in the dish, with bread to dip into the garlicky oil.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away; refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.

recipes.name: Churros con chocolate
recipes.description: Madrid's breakfast treat: crisp, ridged lengths of fried dough dusted with sugar and dunked in thick, spoonable hot chocolate.
equipment: Sturdy piping bag with a 1 cm open-star nozzle, or a churrera

steps.t: Start the chocolate: whisk the cornflour with 100 ml of the cold milk until smooth. Heat the rest of the milk in the saucepan until steaming, then add the chocolate and sugar and whisk until melted.

Whisk in the cornflour mixture and cook over low heat, whisking constantly, for 5–7 minutes, until thick enough to coat a churro, like a pouring custard. Keep it warm on the lowest heat, whisking now and then.

Make the dough: bring the water, salt and olive oil to a rolling boil. Take the pan off the heat, tip in the flour all at once and beat hard with the wooden spoon until a smooth, stiff dough forms and comes away from the sides, about 1 minute. Leave to cool for 5–10 minutes, until you can handle it.
Heat the frying oil in the deep pan (no more than one-third full) to 185 °C. Spoon the dough into the piping bag; it is stiff, so use a sturdy bag.

Pipe 12–15 cm lengths straight into the oil, snipping them off with scissors, and fry 4–5 at a time for 3–4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp. The star-shaped ridges matter: they make churros crunchy and stop them bursting.
Drain on kitchen paper and roll in sugar while still hot. Pour the chocolate into cups and serve straight away, with the churros for dunking.

recipes.storage: Churros are best within an hour of frying. Leftover chocolate keeps for 3 days in the fridge.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp churros in a 200 °C oven for 5 minutes; reheat the chocolate gently, whisking.

recipes.name: Crema catalana
recipes.description: Catalonia's lemon- and cinnamon-scented custard, thickened on the stove with egg yolks and cornflour, chilled in shallow dishes and finished with a crackling layer of burnt sugar.
equipment: Six shallow terracotta dishes or ramekins

ingredients.name: Lemon peel, in wide strips (from 1 lemon)

steps.t: Heat the milk with the lemon peel and cinnamon stick until it just comes to the boil. Turn off the heat, cover and leave to infuse for 15 minutes. Remove the pith from the peel first; it makes the custard bitter.
Whisk the yolks, sugar and cornflour in the bowl until pale and smooth, with no lumps.

Remove the peel and cinnamon and bring the milk back to a simmer. Pour about a third of it onto the yolks, whisking constantly, so they warm up gradually without scrambling, then pour everything back into the pan.

Cook over low-medium heat, stirring constantly in a figure of eight and scraping the base, for 4–6 minutes, until the custard thickly coats the spoon and the first fat bubbles plop on the surface. The cornflour stops it curdling, but don't let it boil hard.
Pour straight into the dishes and tap them to level. Cover the surface with cling film to stop a skin forming, cool and chill for at least 3 hours.

Just before serving, sprinkle each custard with an even layer of sugar and caramelise it with the blowtorch until deep amber and glassy (Catalan cooks use a hot iron). Serve within 30 minutes, while the crust is still crisp.

recipes.storage: @chilled
notes: Traditionally eaten on 19 March, Saint Joseph's Day.
Use the leftover egg whites for meringues.

recipes.name: Marmitako (Basque tuna and potato stew)
recipes.description: The Basque fishermen's stew: potatoes simmered in a sweet pepper and tomato broth until they thicken it, with chunks of fresh tuna added at the very end so they stay tender.

steps.t: Heat the oil in the casserole over medium heat and cook the onion and peppers with a pinch of salt for 12–15 minutes, stirring often, until very soft and sweet.
Add the garlic for 1 minute, then the grated tomato for 5 minutes until jammy. Stir in the paprika (or choricero paste) and the chilli, if using, for 30 seconds.

'Crack' the potatoes into 4 cm chunks: push the knife in a little way and twist so the piece snaps off rather than cutting cleanly. The rough edges release starch that thickens the broth. Add them to the pot and stir for 2 minutes to coat.

Add the stock, bay and salt, bring to the boil and simmer gently, partly covered, for 20–25 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the broth has thickened slightly. Crush a few pieces of potato against the side of the pot to thicken it a little more.

Season the tuna with a pinch of salt. Turn the heat to its lowest (or off), add the tuna, push it under the broth, cover and leave for 5 minutes. The heat of the stew cooks it until just opaque; boiling would make it dry and stringy.
Scatter with parsley, rest for 5 minutes and serve in deep bowls with crusty bread.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently until steaming hot without boiling, so the tuna stays tender.
notes: Choricero peppers are dried sweet Basque peppers; their paste gives a deep, mild flavour. Sweet paprika is the usual substitute.

recipes.name: Pimientos de Padrón (blistered green peppers)
recipes.description: Small green Padrón peppers fried whole in hot olive oil until blistered and soft, then showered with flaky salt. Most are mild, but as the Galician saying goes, some are hot and some are not.

steps.t: Dry the peppers thoroughly, because any water makes the oil spit. Leave the stems on; they are the handle.
Heat the oil in the frying pan over high heat until it shimmers. Add the peppers in a single layer, in two batches if necessary.
Cook for 4–6 minutes, turning them with the tongs or shaking the pan, until the skins are blistered and charred in spots and the peppers are soft and slightly collapsed.
Tip onto a plate, sprinkle generously with flaky salt and serve hot. Eat them by the stem, leaving it behind.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away.

recipes.name: Pa amb tomàquet (Catalan tomato bread)
recipes.description: Catalonia's everyday staple: thick slices of toasted country bread rubbed with garlic and very ripe tomato, drizzled with olive oil and sprinkled with salt.

ingredients.name: Rustic country bread or ciabatta (4 thick slices)

steps.t: Toast the bread on the griddle or under the grill for 2–3 minutes per side, until crisp and golden outside but still soft within.
While it is still hot, rub the cut side of the garlic lightly over the rough surface; the crust grates it like sandpaper. Go easy, as raw garlic is strong.

Rub the cut tomato firmly over the bread, squeezing so the pulp and juice soak in, until only the skin is left in your hand. Alternatively, grate the tomatoes, discard the skins and spoon the pulp over the toast.
Drizzle generously with olive oil, sprinkle with salt and eat at once, on its own for breakfast or alongside cheese, tortilla or grilled vegetables.

recipes.storage: Make just before eating; the bread turns soggy as it stands.

recipes.name: Caldo verde (Portuguese kale and potato soup)
recipes.description: Northern Portugal's beloved soup: a silky purée of potato, onion and garlic simmered with ribbons of couve galega or kale cut as fine as thread, finished with a thread of olive oil.

ingredients.name: Couve galega, collard greens or kale
Extra virgin olive oil, to finish

steps.t: Heat 3 tablespoons of oil in the pot over medium heat and cook the onion for 6–8 minutes until soft and translucent but not browned. Add the garlic for 1 minute.
Add the potatoes, water and salt, bring to the boil and simmer, partly covered, for about 20 minutes, until the potatoes fall apart when pressed.

Meanwhile shred the greens: stack a few leaves, roll them tightly into a cigar and slice across as thinly as you possibly can, 1–2 mm. These fine green threads are what defines caldo verde. Rinse and drain.
Blend the soup until completely smooth and silky. Taste for salt, and thin with a little hot water if needed; it should be like single cream.

If using chouriço, fry the slices in the dry frying pan for 2–3 minutes until the edges crisp and they release their red oil. Bring the soup back to a simmer, add the greens and cook, uncovered, for 3–5 minutes until bright green and just tender. Overcooking turns them khaki.
Ladle into bowls, add a few slices of chouriço if using, and finish each with a thread of olive oil. Serve with Portuguese cornbread (broa) or crusty bread.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: For a halal version, top with slices of smoked beef sausage instead of chouriço.

recipes.name: Bacalhau à Brás (salt cod with straw potatoes and egg)
recipes.description: Lisbon's comfort dish: flaked salt cod and sweet onions tossed with crisp matchstick potatoes and bound with softly scrambled eggs, finished with black olives and parsley.

ingredients.name: Salt cod, dry weight (thick loin pieces)
Potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into fine matchsticks

steps.t: A day or two ahead, rinse the salt cod and put it skin-side up in a large bowl of cold water in the fridge. Change the water 3–4 times a day for 24–48 hours, depending on thickness. Taste a flake: it should be pleasantly seasoned, not harsh. Soaked cod weighs about a third more than dry.

Put the cod in the saucepan, cover with fresh water and bring to a bare simmer; cook for 5 minutes until the flakes separate. Drain and cool slightly, then remove the skin and bones and pull the fish into thin shreds with your fingers.

Make the straw potatoes (batata palha): rinse the matchsticks in cold water and dry them very thoroughly in the tea towel. Heat the frying oil in the deep pan (no more than one-third full) to 175 °C and fry in batches for 3–4 minutes, until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper. You can use 150 g of ready-made potato sticks instead.
Heat the olive oil in the large frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions, garlic and bay for 10–12 minutes, until soft, sweet and pale golden.
Add the cod and stir for 3–4 minutes so it warms through and soaks up the oil. Remove the bay leaf and fold in the potatoes.

Beat the eggs with the pepper, without salt; the cod and potatoes are already salty. Lower the heat, pour in the eggs and stir gently and continuously for 1–2 minutes, until creamy and only just set. Take the pan off the heat while they still look slightly wet; they keep cooking.
Taste for salt, pile onto a warm dish and scatter with the olives and parsley. Serve straight away with a green salad.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away; refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in a frying pan until hot through; the eggs will firm up.
notes: The salt cod is weighed dry, as bought. Soaking removes most of its salt, so the real sodium is lower than calculated.

recipes.name: Frango piri-piri (Portuguese chilli-grilled chicken)
recipes.description: Spatchcocked chicken marinated in a fiery sauce of red chillies, garlic, lemon, paprika and olive oil, then grilled or roasted until charred and juicy and basted with more sauce.
equipment: Barbecue, or oven with a roasting tray and rack

ingredients.name: Fresh red bird's eye (piri-piri) chillies (about 6)
ingredients.prep: use fewer for a milder sauce

steps.t: Spatchcock the chicken: lay it breast-side down and cut along both sides of the backbone with the shears to remove it. Turn it over and press firmly on the breastbone to flatten. Slash the thighs and drumsticks twice to the bone so the marinade gets in and the bird cooks evenly.
Blend the chillies, garlic, paprika, lemon juice, vinegar, oregano, bay and salt with the oil to a coarse sauce. Wash your hands well, or wear gloves, after handling the chillies.
Spoon 4 tablespoons of the sauce into a clean jar for basting and serving. Rub the rest all over the chicken and under the skin. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, or overnight.
Heat the barbecue for indirect medium heat, or the oven to 220 °C. Cook the chicken skin-side up on a rack over the cooler side of the barbecue (or in the oven) for 35–40 minutes.

Brush with half the reserved sauce, then finish skin-side down over direct heat (or under a hot grill) for 5–8 minutes, until the skin is crisp and charred in spots. The thickest part of the thigh should reach 74 °C and the juices run clear.
Rest for 10 minutes, loosely covered. Cut into pieces, drizzle with the remaining sauce and serve with lemon wedges, chips or rice and a tomato salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Keep the basting sauce separate from the raw-chicken marinade.

recipes.name: Pastéis de nata (Portuguese custard tarts)
recipes.description: Lisbon's famous custard tarts: crisp, flaky spiralled pastry cases filled with a lemon- and cinnamon-scented egg custard, baked in a very hot oven until blistered and caramelised on top. Makes 12.

ingredients.name: All-butter puff pastry (1 sheet, about 245 g)

steps.t: Unroll the pastry on a lightly floured surface and roll it up tightly from a short end into a log, like a Swiss roll. Trim the ends and cut it into 12 discs about 2 cm thick. Chill for 15 minutes.

Put one disc, spiral facing up, into each muffin hole. With wet thumbs, press into the centre and push the pastry outwards and up the sides, thinning it so the base is thin and the edge rises a few millimetres above the rim. Chill for 20 minutes.

Make the syrup: heat the sugar, water, cinnamon stick and lemon peel in a small saucepan, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then boil without stirring for 3–4 minutes, until it reaches 105 °C, a light syrup that forms a thin thread. Remove the peel and cinnamon.

Whisk the flour with 60 ml of the cold milk to a smooth paste. Bring the remaining milk to the boil in the second saucepan and whisk it into the paste, then return it all to the pan and cook, whisking, for 2 minutes until thick.
Pour the hot syrup into the milk mixture in a thin stream, whisking. Leave to cool for 10 minutes until warm but not hot, then whisk in the egg yolks and vanilla. Strain into the jug.
Heat the oven to its highest setting (at least 250 °C) with a shelf near the top, for 20 minutes. The tarts need fierce heat to blister.

Fill the pastry cases three-quarters full and bake for 12–16 minutes, until the pastry is golden and crisp and the custard is puffed, with dark, almost burnt blisters on top. Ovens vary, so watch them closely for the last few minutes.
Leave in the tin for 5 minutes, then lift onto a wire rack. Eat warm, dusted with cinnamon and a little icing sugar, as they do in Belém.

recipes.storage: Best on the day. Keep covered at room temperature for up to 1 day, or refrigerate for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Refresh in a 200 °C oven for 5 minutes.
