notes: Freeze the leftover egg whites for meringues or an omelette.

recipes.name: Prego no pão (garlic steak sandwich)
recipes.description: Portugal's favourite snack-bar sandwich: thin steaks rubbed with garlic and bay, seared hot in olive oil, and tucked into a crusty roll with the buttery pan juices and a little mustard.

ingredients.name: Thin beef steaks (sirloin or rump), 4 × 120 g
Dry white wine, in place of the water

steps.t: Lay the steaks between sheets of baking paper and pound them to an even 5 mm thickness. Rub them with the garlic, crumbled bay, salt and pepper and leave for 10 minutes while you prepare the rolls (or up to 2 hours in the fridge).
Split the rolls and warm them in a low oven, or toast the cut sides briefly in the dry frying pan before you cook the meat.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over high heat until it shimmers. Scrape most of the garlic off the steaks and keep it, because it would burn. Sear the steaks two at a time for 45–60 seconds per side, until browned outside and still pink inside, or a little longer if you prefer. Put each steak straight into a roll.
Lower the heat, add the butter, the scraped-off garlic and the water (or wine) to the pan and let it bubble for about a minute, scraping up the browned bits, to make a small amount of sauce.
Spoon the pan juices over the steaks so the bread soaks them up, add mustard or piri-piri sauce if you like, and close the rolls.
Eat hot, with chips or a simple salad. With a fried egg on top it becomes a prego com ovo.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away.
recipes.reheating: Best made to order; reheat leftover steak briefly in a hot pan.

recipes.name: Chicken souvlaki with pita and tzatziki
recipes.description: Greece's favourite street food: chunks of chicken marinated in olive oil, lemon, garlic and oregano, grilled on skewers and wrapped in warm pita with tomato, onion and cool tzatziki.

steps.t: Mix the oil, lemon juice, garlic, oregano, paprika, salt and pepper in the bowl. Add the chicken, toss to coat, cover and refrigerate for 1–4 hours (at least 30 minutes). Lemon tenderises the meat, but left overnight it turns the texture mushy.
If using wooden skewers, soak them in water for 30 minutes so they don't burn.
Make the tzatziki: squeeze the grated cucumber very dry in the tea towel, then mix it with the yoghurt, garlic, oil, dill and salt. Chill until needed; squeezing the cucumber keeps it thick.
Thread the chicken onto the skewers, with the pieces touching but not squashed. Heat the grill pan, barbecue or grill to high.
Grill the skewers for 10–12 minutes, turning every 2–3 minutes, until charred at the edges and cooked through. The juices should run clear and the thickest piece should read 74 °C.
Warm the pitas on the grill for 20–30 seconds per side, until soft and lightly marked.

Spread each pita with tzatziki, add the chicken pulled off the skewers, tomato and onion, and roll up; Athens street stalls tuck in a few chips too. Or serve the skewers on a plate with the pita, salad and lemon wedges.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Pastitsio (Greek baked pasta with meat sauce and béchamel)
recipes.description: Greece's great baked pasta: tubes of pasta bound with egg and cheese, a cinnamon-scented beef and tomato sauce, and a thick, golden layer of nutmeg béchamel, baked until set enough to cut into neat squares.

steps.t: Make the meat sauce: heat the oil in the sauté pan over medium-high heat and cook the onions for 6–8 minutes until soft and golden, then add the garlic for 1 minute. Add the beef, breaking it up, and cook for 8–10 minutes until browned and any liquid has evaporated.

Stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute. Add the wine, if using, and let it bubble away, then add the tomatoes, cinnamon, allspice, bay, salt, pepper and 150 ml of water. Simmer, partly covered, for 30–40 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick and rich with very little liquid. Remove the cinnamon and bay.

Boil the pasta in salted water for 2 minutes less than the packet time; it finishes cooking in the oven. Drain, return to the pot and toss with the melted butter, then with the egg white and 40 g of cheese. This binds the tubes so the slices hold together.

Make the béchamel: melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat, add the flour and whisk for 2 minutes to a pale, bubbling paste (a roux) without letting it brown. Add the warm milk a ladle at a time, whisking out any lumps, then cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until thick enough to coat a spoon heavily. Off the heat, beat in the yolks one at a time, then the cheese, nutmeg and salt.

Heat the oven to 180 °C and butter the dish. Spread half the pasta in an even layer (lay long tubes all in one direction), spread over the meat sauce, then add the rest of the pasta. Pour over the béchamel and smooth it right to the edges.
Bake for 45–50 minutes, until the top is deep golden and bubbling at the edges.
Rest for at least 30 minutes, ideally 45, before cutting; cut too soon, it collapses. Cut into squares and serve warm with a green salad.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze portions for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat, covered, in a 180 °C oven for 20–25 minutes until steaming in the centre.

recipes.name: Gemista (rice-stuffed tomatoes and peppers)
recipes.description: Summer tomatoes and peppers hollowed out and filled with rice cooked in their own pulp with onion, herbs and plenty of olive oil, then baked slowly with potato wedges until soft and caramelised.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 190 °C. Slice the tops off the tomatoes and keep them as lids. Scoop out the flesh with a teaspoon into a bowl, leaving walls about 1 cm thick, sprinkle the insides with a little salt and the sugar and turn upside down to drain. Cut the tops off the peppers, keep them, and pull out the seeds.
Blend or finely chop the scooped tomato flesh to a pulp.

Make the filling: heat 4 tablespoons of the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion for 6–8 minutes until soft, then the garlic for 1 minute. Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes, then add the tomato pulp, tomato paste, half the remaining salt and the pepper. Simmer for 8–10 minutes, until the rice has absorbed most of the liquid but is still very firm; it finishes cooking in the oven. Stir in the parsley and mint.
Stand the tomatoes and peppers upright, snugly, in the roasting dish. Fill each three-quarters full with the rice and some of its liquid, leaving room for the rice to swell, and put the lids back on.

Tuck the potato wedges into the gaps and season them with the rest of the salt. Mix the passata with the water and pour it around the vegetables, not over them, then drizzle the remaining oil over everything.

Cover with foil and bake for 45 minutes. Uncover, baste with the pan juices and bake for 30–40 minutes more, until the rice is tender, the vegetables are soft and wrinkled and the lids and potatoes are browned at the edges. Add a splash of water if the dish dries out.
Rest for at least 20 minutes; gemista are best eaten warm or at room temperature, with feta and bread.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Eat at room temperature, or reheat covered in a 180 °C oven for 20 minutes until hot through.

recipes.name: Fasolada (Greek white bean soup)
recipes.description: The soup often called Greece's national dish: white beans simmered with carrot, celery, onion and tomato in a broth enriched with plenty of olive oil, finished with lemon and parsley.

steps.t: If using dried beans, as Greek cooks traditionally do, soak 300 g overnight in plenty of cold water. Drain, cover with fresh water, boil for 10 minutes, then simmer for 45–60 minutes until almost tender, and drain. Use them in place of the canned beans.
Heat 60 ml of the oil in the pot over medium heat and cook the onion, carrot and celery for about 10 minutes, until soft and starting to colour.
Add the garlic for 1 minute, then stir in the tomato paste for 1–2 minutes until it darkens, and add the tomatoes.

Add the beans, water, bay and oregano and simmer, partly covered, for 35–40 minutes, until the vegetables are very tender and the broth has thickened. Crush a ladleful of beans against the side of the pot to make it creamier.
Season with the salt and pepper, then stir in the remaining oil and the lemon juice. Greek cooks add the oil generously at the end; it gives the soup its richness.
Scatter with parsley and serve hot with bread, feta, olives and a little raw onion on the side, the classic Lenten meal.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 4 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Tzatziki (yoghurt, cucumber and garlic dip)
recipes.description: Thick strained yoghurt mixed with grated, well-squeezed cucumber, garlic, olive oil, a dash of vinegar and dill: the cool dip and sauce served with grilled meat, souvlaki and bread all over Greece.

ingredients.name: Cucumber (1)
ingredients.prep: coarsely grated, seeds scooped out if large

steps.t: Toss the grated cucumber with the salt and leave for 10 minutes, then squeeze it hard in the tea towel to remove as much water as you can. Dry cucumber keeps tzatziki thick instead of runny.
Crush the garlic to a smooth paste with a pinch of salt, or grate it finely. Start with one clove and add more to taste; it gets stronger as it sits.
Mix the yoghurt, cucumber, garlic, vinegar and dill in the bowl, then beat in the olive oil until glossy.
Serve straight away, or chill for 30 minutes if you have time so the garlic mellows. Finish with a thread of oil and a few olives, and serve with pita, souvlaki, grilled fish or vegetables.

recipes.storage: Keeps covered in the fridge for up to 4 days.

recipes.name: Kotosoupa avgolemono (chicken, rice and egg-lemon soup)
recipes.description: The Greek cure-all: chicken simmered into a clear broth with rice, then thickened off the heat with eggs whisked with lemon juice into a silky, tangy, pale-gold soup.

ingredients.name: Chicken thighs and drumsticks, bone-in, skinless

steps.t: Put the chicken, water, onion, carrot, celery, bay and salt in the pot and bring slowly to the boil, skimming off the grey foam as it rises so the broth stays clear. Simmer gently, partly covered, for 45 minutes, until the chicken is falling off the bone.
Lift out the chicken and strain the broth; you should have about 1.6 litres. Discard the vegetables. When the chicken is cool enough to handle, shred it and discard the bones.
Return the broth to the pot, bring it to the boil and add the rice. Simmer for 15–18 minutes until very tender.

Make the avgolemono: whisk the eggs in the large bowl for 1–2 minutes until frothy, then whisk in the lemon juice. Whisking constantly, add 3–4 ladles of the hot broth one at a time; warming the eggs gradually like this (tempering) stops them curdling.

Take the pot off the heat and pour in the egg mixture, stirring constantly. Return it to low heat and stir for 2–3 minutes, until the soup thickens slightly and turns silky. Don't let it boil, or the eggs will scramble.
Stir the chicken back in (or serve it on the side, as many Greek families do), season with pepper and more lemon or salt to taste, and serve at once, with dill if you like.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently over low heat, stirring, until steaming; don't let it boil or the egg will curdle.

recipes.name: Strapatsada (Greek scrambled eggs with tomato and feta)
recipes.description: Ripe grated tomatoes cooked down in olive oil until jammy, then stirred with eggs into soft, creamy curds and finished with crumbled feta and oregano, eaten with bread.

steps.t: Halve the tomatoes and grate the cut sides on the coarse side of the box grater until only the skin is left in your hand. Discard the skins.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat, add the tomato pulp and salt and simmer for 8–10 minutes, stirring, until most of the liquid has evaporated and the tomato is thick and jammy, with oil separating at the edges. Concentrating the tomato first stops the eggs turning watery.
Beat the eggs lightly with the pepper; feta is salty, so they need little or no salt.
Lower the heat to medium-low and pour in the eggs. Leave for 20 seconds, then stir slowly, folding into large curds, for 2–3 minutes, until softly set but still glossy.
Take the pan off the heat and fold in most of the feta; it softens without melting completely.
Serve straight from the pan, topped with the rest of the feta and the oregano, with crusty bread and a few olives.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away.

recipes.name: Shepherd's pie
recipes.description: Minced lamb slow-cooked with onion, carrot, thyme and stock into a rich gravy, topped with buttery mashed potato and baked until the ridges are crisp and golden.

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (Maris Piper or russet)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into even chunks

steps.t: Heat the oil in the sauté pan over high heat. Add the lamb in two batches, spreading it flat and leaving it undisturbed for 3–4 minutes until a brown crust forms, then break it up and cook until browned all over. Tip into a sieve to drain off the excess fat. Browned, not grey, mince is where the flavour comes from.
Lower the heat to medium and cook the onion, carrot and celery in a spoonful of the fat for 8–10 minutes until softened. Add the garlic for 1 minute.

Stir in the tomato paste and flour for 1–2 minutes. Return the lamb, then add the Worcestershire sauce, wine (if using), stock, thyme, salt and pepper. Simmer gently, partly covered, for 30–40 minutes, stirring now and then, until the gravy is thick and glossy and coats the meat rather than pooling. Stir in the peas, remove the herb stalks and spread the filling in the baking dish to cool slightly.
Meanwhile cover the potatoes with cold salted water, bring to the boil and simmer for 15–20 minutes until completely tender. Drain well and leave them in the hot pan for 2 minutes to steam dry.
Mash or rice the potatoes with the butter and warm milk until smooth and fluffy, and season with the salt. Don't overwork them, or the mash turns gluey.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Spoon the mash over the filling, starting around the edges to seal it in, then spread it over and rough up the surface with a fork; the ridges turn crisp in the oven.
Bake for 25–30 minutes, until the top is golden and the filling bubbles up at the edges. Rest for 10 minutes and serve with peas or buttered greens.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze, baked or unbaked, for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat, covered, in a 180 °C oven for 30–40 minutes until piping hot in the centre.
notes: Shepherds keep sheep, so shepherd's pie is made with lamb; made with beef it is cottage pie.

recipes.name: Cottage pie
recipes.description: The beef version of shepherd's pie: minced beef braised with onion, carrot, celery, tomato and Worcestershire sauce under a mustardy mashed potato lid with a crisp layer of Cheddar.

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into even chunks

steps.t: Heat the oil in the sauté pan over high heat and brown the beef in two batches, pressing it flat and leaving it for a few minutes to colour before breaking it up. Lift out with a slotted spoon, leaving most of the fat behind.

Turn the heat down to medium and soften the onion, carrot and celery in the pan for 8–10 minutes, scraping up the browned bits as the vegetables release their juices. Add the garlic for the last minute.

Stir in the tomato paste and flour and cook for 2 minutes until the paste darkens. Return the beef and add the Worcestershire sauce, stock, bay, thyme, salt and pepper. Simmer, partly covered, for 30–40 minutes, until thick enough that a spoon dragged through leaves a clear trail. Discard the bay leaf and spread the filling in the dish.
While the beef simmers, boil the potatoes in salted water for 15–20 minutes until tender all the way through, then drain and steam dry in the pan for 2 minutes.
Mash the potatoes with the butter, warm milk, mustard and salt until smooth. The mustard gives the mash a gentle warmth that suits beef.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Spread the mash over the beef, sealing the edges, fork the top into ridges and scatter over the Cheddar.
Bake for 25–30 minutes, until the cheese is bubbling and deep golden and the gravy bubbles at the edges. Leave to settle for 10 minutes, then serve with peas, carrots or greens.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze, baked or unbaked, for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat, covered, in a 180 °C oven for 30–40 minutes until piping hot in the centre.

recipes.name: Fish and chips
recipes.description: Thick fillets of cod or haddock in a light, crisp batter, served with chunky double-cooked chips, lemon and a splash of malt vinegar, the way British chip shops do it.
equipment: Large deep heavy pan or deep-fryer
Wire rack set over a tray

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (Maris Piper or russet)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 1.5 cm chips

ingredients.name: Sunflower or vegetable oil, for deep-frying (for chips and fish)
Thick cod or haddock fillets, skinless (4 × 170 g)
Ice-cold lager, in place of the water

steps.t: Rinse the chips under cold water to wash off the surface starch, then simmer them in salted water for 4–5 minutes, until just tender at the edges but holding their shape. Drain carefully, spread on a tray and leave to dry and cool for 15 minutes. Dry chips fry crisper and spit less.
Heat the oil in the deep pan (no more than one-third full) to 140 °C. Fry the chips in two batches for 6–8 minutes, until soft and pale but not coloured. Lift onto the rack.

Pat the fish completely dry and season with half the salt. Whisk the batter flour, baking powder and the rest of the salt in the bowl, then whisk in the ice-cold sparkling water (or lager) until smooth and as thick as double cream; a few small lumps are fine. Use it straight away, while the bubbles keep it light.

Raise the oil to 180 °C. Dust each fillet in flour so the batter clings, dip it in the batter and let the excess drip off, then lower it into the oil away from you, laying it in gently. Fry two at a time for 6–8 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp and the fish flakes easily (63 °C in the centre). Drain on the rack and keep warm in a 120 °C oven.
Let the oil come back to 180 °C and fry the chips in batches for 3–4 minutes, until deep golden and crisp. Drain and salt immediately.
Serve at once with lemon wedges and malt vinegar, and mushy peas or tartare sauce on the side.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 220 °C oven for 10–12 minutes.

recipes.name: Irish stew
recipes.description: Ireland's simplest, most comforting stew: lamb simmered slowly with onions, carrots and two kinds of potato, some melting to thicken the broth and some staying whole, finished with parsley.
equipment: Large heavy casserole with a lid

ingredients.name: Lamb neck fillet or boneless shoulder
ingredients.prep: cut into 4 cm chunks, excess fat trimmed

steps.t: Season the lamb with half the salt and the pepper. Traditional Irish stew is not browned, which gives a pale, clean-tasting broth. For a deeper flavour, brown the lamb in the oil in batches over medium-high heat for 6–8 minutes.
Layer the casserole: the sliced floury potatoes on the bottom, then the lamb, onions and carrots (and the barley, if using), seasoning each layer with a little of the remaining salt.
Pour in the stock to just cover, add the thyme and bay and bring slowly to the boil, skimming off any grey foam from the surface.
Cover and simmer very gently over low heat, or in a 160 °C oven, for 1 hour. The liquid should barely tremble; hard boiling toughens the meat.

Add the waxy potatoes on top, pushing them into the liquid, cover again and cook for 40–50 minutes more, until the lamb is meltingly tender and the floury potatoes underneath have collapsed and thickened the broth.
Skim the fat from the surface, remove the herbs, and taste for salt and pepper. Stir in the parsley and rest for 10 minutes. Serve in deep bowls with soda bread and butter.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate for up to 3 days; it tastes even better the next day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Carrots divide opinion: many families in the west of Ireland leave them out.

recipes.name: Colcannon (Irish mash with kale and spring onions)
recipes.description: Ireland's buttery mashed potatoes folded with softened kale or cabbage and spring onions warmed in milk, served with a pool of melting butter in the middle.

steps.t: Put the potatoes in a saucepan of cold salted water, bring to the boil and simmer for 15–18 minutes until completely tender. Drain and return to the pan over low heat for a minute to steam off the excess water.
Meanwhile melt 20 g of the butter in the frying pan, add the kale or cabbage with a splash of water and cook for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until tender and bright green.
Warm the milk with the spring onions in the small pan for 2–3 minutes, until just simmering; this softens the onions and flavours the milk.
Mash the potatoes with another 20 g of butter, then gradually beat in the hot milk and spring onions until smooth and creamy. Fold in the greens and season with the pepper and more salt if needed.
Pile into a warm dish, make a well in the centre and drop in the remaining butter to melt into a golden pool. Serve with sausages, roast chicken or a fried egg.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a covered dish until hot, or fry leftovers into crisp potato cakes.
notes: Colcannon is traditionally eaten at Halloween in Ireland, sometimes with a coin or ring hidden inside.

recipes.name: Welsh rarebit (cheese on toast with mustard sauce)
recipes.description: Far more than cheese on toast: a thick, savoury sauce of mature Cheddar, butter, mustard and Worcestershire sauce spread over toast and grilled until bubbling and golden-brown.

ingredients.name: Ale or stout, in place of the milk
Thick slices of good white or brown bread (4)

steps.t: Melt the butter in the saucepan over medium-low heat, stir in the flour and cook for 1 minute. Gradually stir in the milk (or ale) and cook for about 2 minutes, stirring, until smooth and thick.

Turn the heat to its lowest and stir in the cheese until melted into a thick paste, then beat in the mustard, Worcestershire sauce and cayenne, and finally the egg yolk. It should be spreadable, not runny. Don't let it boil, or the cheese turns oily and stringy.
Heat the grill to high. Toast the bread on one side under the grill, then turn and lightly toast the other side.

Spread the cheese mixture thickly over the lightly toasted sides, right to the edges so the crusts don't burn, and grill for 2–4 minutes until bubbling and browned in spots. Serve at once with an extra dash of Worcestershire sauce.

recipes.storage: The cheese mixture keeps for 3 days in the fridge; spread and grill to order.

recipes.name: Scones
recipes.description: Light, tall British scones rubbed together from flour, butter and milk and baked until risen and golden, served warm with jam and clotted cream for afternoon tea. Makes about 10.
equipment: Baking tray lined with baking paper

ingredients.name: Clotted cream or whipped double cream, to serve

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220 °C and line the tray. Sift the flour, baking powder and salt into the bowl.
Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips, lifting the mixture high to aerate it, until it looks like fine breadcrumbs with no lumps of butter. Stir in the sugar.

Make a well, pour in most of the milk and mix quickly with a table knife into a soft, slightly sticky dough, adding the rest of the milk if there are dry patches. Handle it as little as possible; overworked dough makes tough, flat scones.
Tip onto a floured surface and fold it over 2–3 times just to smooth it, then pat it out (don't roll) to 3 cm thick.

Dip the cutter in flour and press it straight down firmly without twisting; twisting seals the edges and stops the scones rising. Place them close together on the tray. Gently press the trimmings together and cut more, to make about 10.
Brush the tops only with beaten egg, not the sides. Bake for 12–15 minutes, until well risen and golden; they should sound hollow when tapped underneath.
Cool on the rack wrapped in a clean tea towel, which keeps them soft. Serve warm, split by hand, with jam and clotted cream: cream first in Devon, jam first in Cornwall.

recipes.storage: Best on the day. Keep in an airtight tin for up to 2 days, or freeze for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a 160 °C oven for 5 minutes.

recipes.name: Sticky toffee pudding
recipes.description: A light, moist sponge made dark and fudgy with chopped dates and muscovado sugar, soaked in a buttery toffee sauce and served warm with more sauce and cream.
equipment: 20 cm square baking tin, greased and lined

ingredients.name: Dark muscovado or soft brown sugar
Dark muscovado or soft brown sugar
Pouring cream or vanilla ice cream

steps.t: Heat the oven to 180 °C and grease and line the tin. Simmer the dates in the boiling water for 3–4 minutes until soft, then take off the heat and stir in the bicarbonate of soda; it will foam up. This softens the dates and darkens the sponge. Leave to cool for 10 minutes.

Beat the butter and sugar with the electric whisk for about 3 minutes until fluffy. Beat in the eggs one at a time, adding a spoonful of the flour with each to stop the mixture curdling, then the vanilla.
Fold in the remaining flour and the baking powder, then the date mixture with its liquid, to make a loose batter. Mash the dates first, or blend them, for a smoother pudding.
Pour into the tin and bake for 30–35 minutes, until risen and springy, and a skewer pushed into the centre comes out clean.
Meanwhile make the sauce: melt the butter, sugar, half the cream and the salt in the saucepan over medium heat, stirring, then boil for 3–4 minutes until dark and glossy. Stir in the remaining cream.

While the pudding is still hot, prick it all over with the skewer and pour over a third of the sauce. Leave for 10 minutes to soak in, then cut into squares and serve warm with the rest of the sauce and cream or ice cream.

recipes.storage: Keep covered at room temperature for 1 day or in the fridge for up to 4 days. Freezes well with its sauce for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat portions, covered, in a 160 °C oven for 15 minutes, or in the microwave until hot; warm the sauce separately.

recipes.name: Kedgeree (smoked haddock, rice and egg)
recipes.description: The Victorian country-house breakfast: buttery, curry-spiced rice folded with flakes of poached smoked haddock and topped with soft-boiled eggs, parsley and lemon.
equipment: Wide frying pan with a lid

ingredients.name: Basmati rice
ingredients.prep: rinsed until the water runs clear

ingredients.name: Lemon
ingredients.prep: half juiced, half cut into wedges

steps.t: Lay the haddock skin-side up in the frying pan with the milk, bay leaf and enough water just to cover. Bring to a bare simmer, cover, turn off the heat and leave for 8–10 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes easily. Lift it out, keep 4 tablespoons of the poaching liquid, and flake the fish into large pieces, discarding the skin and any bones.
Cook the rice in plenty of boiling salted water for 10–12 minutes until just tender, then drain well.
Lower the eggs into a pan of simmering water and cook for 7–8 minutes for jammy yolks. Cool them in cold water, then peel and quarter.

Melt the butter in the wide pan over medium-low heat and cook the onion for 8–10 minutes until soft and golden. Add the curry powder and turmeric and stir for 1 minute, until fragrant; cooking spices in fat like this (blooming) releases their flavour.

Add the rice and toss until every grain is coated and golden. Add the reserved poaching liquid, then gently fold in the fish and heat for 2–3 minutes, until steaming hot, taking care not to break up the flakes.

Season with pepper and the lemon juice, and taste before adding salt; smoked fish is already salty. Fold in most of the parsley, top with the eggs and the rest of the parsley and serve with lemon wedges, and mango chutney if you like.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 1 hour and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Undyed smoked haddock is best; smoked cod, hot-smoked salmon or hot-smoked trout also work.

recipes.name: Scottish porridge
recipes.description: Proper Scottish porridge: oats simmered slowly with water, a little milk and a pinch of salt, stirred until thick and creamy, and served with cold milk and a little brown sugar or honey.

ingredients.name: Rolled oats (or pinhead oatmeal, soaked overnight)

steps.t: For a nuttier flavour, toast the oats in the dry saucepan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until they smell like biscuits. This step is optional.
Add the water and milk and bring to the boil over medium heat, stirring.

Lower the heat to a gentle simmer and cook for 8–10 minutes (20–25 minutes for soaked pinhead oatmeal), stirring often with the spurtle or spoon and scraping the base so it doesn't catch. It is ready when thick and creamy and the oats are soft. Add a splash of water if it gets too thick.
Stir in the salt for the last couple of minutes. Many Scots say salt added at the start toughens the oats; at the end it brings out their flavour without making the porridge taste salty.
Take the pan off the heat and leave for a minute to thicken slightly, then pour into warm bowls.
Serve the traditional way, with a separate cup of cold milk to dip each spoonful into, or with a sprinkle of brown sugar or a drizzle of honey and a handful of berries.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate leftovers for up to 2 days; porridge sets firm as it cools.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with a splash of milk or water, stirring, until hot and creamy.

recipes.name: Boerenkool stamppot (kale and potato mash with smoked sausage)
recipes.description: The Dutch winter classic: floury potatoes boiled with plenty of chopped curly kale, mashed together with milk and butter, and served with smoked sausage, mustard and a well of gravy or butter.

ingredients.name: Dutch or Dijon mustard, to serve

steps.t: Put the potatoes and salt in the large pot with just enough water to barely cover them and bring to the boil.

Pile the chopped kale on top of the potatoes; it looks like a lot but wilts down. Cover and cook over medium heat for about 20 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the kale is soft. The kale steams on top rather than boiling.

Meanwhile put the sausages in a saucepan of hot water and keep it just below a simmer for 15–20 minutes, until heated right through; boiling splits the skins. If using lardons, fry them in a dry pan until crisp.

Drain the potatoes and kale well, keeping a cupful of the cooking water. Return them to the pot, add the butter and warm milk and mash everything together roughly; stamppot should be rustic, not a smooth purée. Season with the nutmeg, pepper and more salt to taste, loosening it with cooking water if stiff. Stir in the lardons, if using.
Slice the sausages into thick pieces, or leave them whole to lay on top.
Heap the stamppot onto warm plates, make a small well (a kuiltje) in the centre for gravy or a knob of butter, add the sausage and serve with mustard, and pickled gherkins or onions on the side.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a pan with a splash of milk, stirring, until steaming hot.
safety: Heat smoked sausage gently until steaming hot throughout (74 °C / 165 °F).
notes: Rookworst is usually pork; halal beef rookworst is widely sold in the Netherlands.

recipes.name: Hutspot met klapstuk (carrot and onion mash with braised beef)
recipes.description: Leiden's hutspot: potatoes, carrots and onions boiled together and mashed coarsely with butter, served with slow-braised beef (klapstuk) and its gravy, as eaten every 3 October to mark the end of the 1574 siege.

ingredients.name: Beef flank or chuck (klapstuk), in one piece

steps.t: Season the beef with the salt and pepper. Melt the butter in the casserole over medium-high heat and brown the meat on all sides for 8–10 minutes, until deep brown.

Add the sliced onion, bay and cloves and cook for 3 minutes, then pour in enough stock to come halfway up the meat. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook very gently over low heat for 2–2½ hours, turning the beef once, until tender enough to pull apart with a fork. Top up with water if it gets low.

About 45 minutes before the beef is ready, put the carrots in the large pot, then the onions, then the potatoes on top. Add water to just cover the carrots, and the salt; cover, bring to the boil and simmer for 25–30 minutes, until everything is tender. The potatoes steam on top.

Drain, keeping a cup of the cooking liquid. Mash with the butter and warm milk, keeping it coarse: hutspot should be flecked with orange, not a smooth purée. Season with the nutmeg and more salt and pepper, loosening with cooking liquid if needed.
Lift the beef out and rest it for 10 minutes. Meanwhile boil the braising liquid for about 5 minutes to reduce it into a thin gravy, remove the bay and cloves and taste for seasoning.
Slice or pull the beef into chunks and serve it on the hutspot, with a well of gravy in each portion.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Hutspot is also good on its own with a fried egg, or with smoked sausage as in the boerenkool version.

recipes.name: Moules-frites (mussels with Belgian fries)
recipes.description: Belgium's national dish: a big pot of mussels steamed open with celery, onion, butter and herbs, served in their broth alongside crisp, twice-fried frites and mayonnaise.
equipment: Very large pot with a tight lid

ingredients.name: Floury potatoes (Bintje or Maris Piper)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 1 cm chips

ingredients.name: Dry white wine, in place of the water (moules marinières)

steps.t: Clean the mussels: rinse them in cold water, pull off the beards (the stringy tufts) by tugging towards the hinge and scrape off any barnacles. Tap any open mussels sharply on the counter and discard those that don't close, along with any with cracked shells. Keep them in the fridge in a colander covered with a damp cloth.

First fry for the frites: rinse the chips and dry them very thoroughly. Heat the oil (no more than one-third of the pan) to 150 °C and fry in batches for 5–6 minutes, until soft and pale but not coloured. Drain on the rack and leave for at least 15 minutes; this first fry cooks the inside.
Melt the butter in the very large pot over medium heat and cook the onion and celery for 5 minutes until soft, then add the garlic, thyme and bay for 1 minute.
Heat the frying oil to 180 °C for the second fry.

Turn the heat under the mussel pot to high, add the mussels and the water (or wine), cover tightly and cook for 4–6 minutes, shaking the pot hard every minute, until the shells have opened wide. Don't overcook, or the mussels shrink and toughen. Discard any that stay closed.
While the mussels steam, fry the frites a second time, in batches, for 2–3 minutes until deep golden and crisp. Drain and salt at once.

Season the mussels with pepper, scatter over the parsley and toss. Serve in deep bowls with their broth, the frites alongside, mayonnaise for dipping and an empty bowl for the shells; an empty shell makes a handy pair of tongs.

recipes.storage: Eat mussels on the day they are cooked; refrigerate leftovers within 1 hour and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Reheat leftover mussels gently in their broth just until hot; re-crisp frites in a 220 °C oven.

recipes.name: Gaufres de Liège (Liège sugar waffles)
recipes.description: Belgium's street waffle: a rich, buttery yeasted dough studded with pearl sugar, cooked in a hot waffle iron until the sugar caramelises into crunchy pockets on a soft, chewy waffle. Makes about 14.
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl

ingredients.name: Belgian pearl sugar (or roughly crushed sugar cubes)

steps.t: Stir the yeast and a teaspoon of the sugar into the lukewarm milk and leave for 5–10 minutes until foamy.
Put the flour, the rest of the 30 g of sugar and the salt in the mixer bowl. Add the yeast mixture, eggs and vanilla and knead with the dough hook on low speed for 5 minutes to a soft, sticky dough.

Add the butter a few pieces at a time, letting each be absorbed before adding more, then knead for 5 minutes more until the dough is glossy, smooth and elastic. By hand, squeeze the butter in and then slap and fold the dough on the counter for about 10 minutes.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 1–1½ hours, until doubled in size.
Knead in the pearl sugar gently by hand until evenly spread; a mixer would crush it. Divide into about 14 balls of 80 g and leave on a tray for 15 minutes.

Heat the waffle iron to medium-high, about 180 °C; hotter, and the sugar burns before the dough is cooked. Put a ball in the centre of each section, close the lid and cook for 3–4 minutes, until deep golden with caramelised patches.

Lift out carefully with tongs, because the melted sugar is very hot, and cool on the rack for 2 minutes. Eat warm and plain; they need no toppings. Scrape caramelised sugar off the iron between batches with a wooden skewer.

recipes.storage: Keep cooled waffles in an airtight container for up to 2 days, or freeze for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a 180 °C oven or a toaster for 3–4 minutes until crisp.
notes: Pearl sugar (sucre perlé) doesn't melt completely in the dough; crushed sugar cubes are the usual substitute.
